title: Job

stories.title: 🕊️ Job 1
summaryBullets: There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. And this man was blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil. (1:1).
He had seven sons and three daughters, (1:2).
and he owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, 500 female donkeys, and a very large number of servants. Job was the greatest man of all the people of the East. (1:3).
Job’s sons would take turns holding feasts in their homes, and they would invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them. (1:4).

And when the days of feasting were over, Job would send for his children to purify them, rising early in the morning to offer burnt offerings for all of them. For Job thought, “Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts.” This was Job’s regular practice. (1:5).
One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came with them. (1:6).
“Where have you come from?” said the LORD to Satan. “From roaming through the earth,” he replied, “and walking back and forth in it.” (1:7).
Then the LORD said to Satan, “Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil.” (1:8).
Satan answered the LORD, “Does Job fear God for nothing? (1:9).
Have You not placed a hedge on every side around him and his household and all that he owns? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land. (1:10).
But stretch out Your hand and strike all that he has, and he will surely curse You to Your face.” (1:11).
“Very well,” said the LORD to Satan. “Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself.” Then Satan went out from the presence of the LORD. (1:12).
One day, while Job’s sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house, (1:13).
a messenger came and reported to Job: “While the oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing nearby, (1:14).
the Sabeans swooped down and took them away. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you!” (1:15).
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and reported: “The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants, and I alone have escaped to tell you!” (1:16).

While he was still speaking, another messenger came and reported: “The Chaldeans formed three bands, raided the camels, and took them away. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you!” (1:17).
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and reported: “Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house, (1:18).
when suddenly a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you!” (1:19).
Then Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped, (1:20).
saying: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD.” (1:21).
In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing. (1:22).
crossRefs: Ezekiel 14:14-20: Job named beside Noah and Daniel as a man whose righteousness would deliver only himself.
James 5:11: Job held up by name as the example of a man who endured and saw what the Lord finally did.
1 Kings 22:19-23: A prophet sees the LORD enthroned with the host of heaven standing to His right and left.
Genesis 13:2: Abraham's wealth reckoned the same way Job's is, in livestock and silver and gold.
Zechariah 3:1-2: The accuser stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest and is rebuked by the LORD.

translationNotes.note: A real region east or southeast of Canaan, not a nowhere. Lamentations 4:21 places the daughter of Edom dwelling in the land of Uz, and Jeremiah 25:20 lists the kings of Uz among the nations near Edom, Philistia and Arabia. Job's neighbours in the book are Sabean and Chaldean raiders and friends from Teman in Edom, which fits the same stretch of country on the desert edge east of the Jordan and south toward Arabia.

7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen and 500 female donkeys (1:3). For scale, the largest single herd transfer in Genesis is Jacob's gift to Esau, and it counts 550 head plus the camels' young, of which only 30 were milk camels (Genesis 32:14-15). Job's camel herd alone is a hundred times the camels in that gift. In a world with no coinage, this was the whole of a man's capital, walking, and it could be driven off in an afternoon, which is exactly what happens in verses 14 to 17.

A tzemed is a matched pair harnessed to one plough, the working unit of a ploughman. 500 yoke means 1,000 oxen and 500 ploughs able to work the same day. When Elijah finds Elisha, a man wealthy enough to burn his gear and slaughter his team, he is ploughing with twelve yoke (1 Kings 19:19). Job's operation is more than forty times that.

The people of Sheba in southwest Arabia, in what is now Yemen, who controlled the overland incense road that carried frankincense and myrrh north to Egypt and Mesopotamia. Their queen visits Solomon in 1 Kings 10:1-13, and Job himself names their caravans at 6:19. Caravan states raided as well as traded; these are not desert nobodies but the wealthiest merchant power in Arabia.

Tribal groups of southern Mesopotamia, in the marsh country near the head of the Persian Gulf. Abraham came from Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 11:28). Here they are still raiders working in three bands (1:17), centuries before their dynasty took Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar burned Jerusalem.

Ripping the outer garment down the front was the standard public signal of grief or horror across the ancient Near East, done at the moment the news lands. Jacob does it for Joseph (Genesis 37:34), David for Saul (2 Samuel 1:11), and the high priest at Jesus' trial (Matthew 26:65). Shaving the head belongs to the same set of mourning acts (Isaiah 15:2; Micah 1:16). Job performs the full ritual and then worships, which is the point of verse 21.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job, a wealthy and righteous man in Uz, loses his livestock, servants, and all ten children in a series of catastrophes after Satan challenges God that Job only serves him for protection and prosperity. Job tears his robe and shaves his head in grief but worships God and does not curse him.

headings.text: Job Loses His Children and Possessions

stories.title: 🕊️ Job 2
summaryBullets: On another day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came with them to present himself before Him. (2:1).
“Where have you come from?” said the LORD to Satan. “From roaming through the earth,” he replied, “and walking back and forth in it.” (2:2).

Then the LORD said to Satan, “Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil. He still retains his integrity, even though you incited Me against him to ruin him without cause.” (2:3).
“Skin for skin!” Satan replied. “A man will give up all he owns in exchange for his life. (2:4).
But stretch out Your hand and strike his flesh and bones, and he will surely curse You to Your face.” (2:5).
“Very well,” said the LORD to Satan. “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life.” (2:6).
So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and infected Job with terrible boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head. (2:7).
And Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself as he sat among the ashes. (2:8).
Then Job’s wife said to him, “Do you still retain your integrity? Curse God and die!” (2:9).
“You speak as a foolish woman speaks,” he told her. “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” In all this, Job did not sin in what he said. (2:10).

Now when Job’s three friends— Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite— heard about all this adversity that had come upon him, each of them came from his home, and they met together to go and sympathize with Job and comfort him. (2:11).
When they lifted up their eyes from afar, they could barely recognize Job. They began to weep aloud, and each man tore his robe and threw dust in the air over his head. (2:12).
Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was. (2:13).
crossRefs: Genesis 50:10: Joseph mourns seven days for his father at the threshing floor of Atad beyond the Jordan.
1 Samuel 31:13: The men of Jabesh bury Saul's bones under the tamarisk and fast seven days.
Ezekiel 3:15: Ezekiel sits among the exiles at Tel-abib seven days, overwhelmed and silent.
Isaiah 30:14: A potsherd is what is left to scoop fire from a hearth or water from a cistern.
Deuteronomy 28:27,35: Boils from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head named among the covenant curses.

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew carries the definite article: not a personal name but a title, the accuser or the adversary, the one who brings the charge. The same noun without the article is used of ordinary human opponents: the Philistine commanders fear David will become a satan to them in battle (1 Samuel 29:4), and Hadad and Rezon are each called a satan to Solomon (1 Kings 11:14,23).

Every settlement had a mound outside it where hearth ash and refuse were dumped and burned. The Greek translation of Job made around the second century BC reads that he sat on the dung heap outside the city. Sitting in ash was also the recognised posture of mourning and self-abasement (2 Samuel 13:19; Esther 4:1-3; Jeremiah 6:26). Job is at once diseased, ritually excluded and in mourning, and he is sitting in the town's rubbish.

The commonest object underfoot in any ancient town. Fired clay does not rot, so broken jars littered every surface, and people picked up sherds to scrape, to carry embers, to dip water (Isaiah 30:14) and to write on. Thousands of such written sherds survive, including the Lachish letters from the last days before Jerusalem fell. Job has no physician and no salve; he is using free rubbish on open sores.

A trader's phrase, the language of hide swapped for hide in a market. The accuser's own gloss follows in the same verse: a man will give up everything he owns to keep his life (2:4). The argument is that Job's losses in chapter 1 cost him only property, and the real test is his own body.

Seven days was the fixed mourning period for the dead. Joseph mourns Jacob seven days (Genesis 50:10), the men of Jabesh fast seven days for Saul (1 Samuel 31:13), and Ezekiel sits seven days among the exiles (Ezekiel 3:15). Custom held that the mourners stay silent until the sufferer speaks first. The friends are keeping the rite for a dead man while Job is still alive, and their silence is not awkwardness but the correct form.

stories.keyTakeaway: Satan challenges God that Job will curse him if afflicted in body rather than possessions; God allows Satan to strike Job with sores, Job's wife urges him to curse God, and his three friends arrive to sit with him in silence.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 3
summaryBullets: After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth. (3:1).
And this is what he said: (3:2).
“May the day of my birth perish, and the night it was said, ‘A boy is conceived.’ (3:3).
If only that day had turned to darkness! May God above disregard it; may no light shine upon it. (3:4).
May darkness and gloom reclaim it, and a cloud settle over it; may the blackness of the day overwhelm it. (3:5).
If only darkness had taken that night away! May it not appear among the days of the year; may it never be entered in any of the months. (3:6).
Behold, may that night be barren; may no joyful voice come into it. (3:7).
May it be cursed by those who curse the day — those prepared to rouse Leviathan. (3:8).
May its morning stars grow dark; may it wait in vain for daylight; may it not see the breaking of dawn. (3:9).
For that night did not shut the doors of the womb to hide the sorrow from my eyes. (3:10).
Why did I not perish at birth; why did I not die as I came from the womb? (3:11).
Why were there knees to receive me, and breasts that I should be nursed? (3:12).
For now I would be lying down in peace; I would be asleep and at rest (3:13).
with kings and counselors of the earth, who built for themselves cities now in ruins, (3:14).
or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver. (3:15).
Or why was I not hidden like a stillborn child, like an infant who never sees daylight? (3:16).
There the wicked cease from raging, and there the weary find rest. (3:17).
The captives enjoy their ease; they do not hear the voice of the oppressor. (3:18).
Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master. (3:19).
Why is light given to the miserable, and life to the bitter of soul, (3:20).
who long for death that does not come, and search for it like hidden treasure, (3:21).
who rejoice and greatly exult when they reach the grave? (3:22).
Why is life given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in? (3:23).
I sigh when food is put before me, and my groans pour out like water. (3:24).
For the thing I feared has overtaken me, and what I dreaded has befallen me. (3:25).
I am not at ease or quiet; I have no rest, for trouble has come.” (3:26).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 20:14-18: Jeremiah curses the day he was born and the man who carried the news to his father.
Psalm 88:3-7: A prayer out of the pit, from a man counted with the dead and given no relief at all.
Ecclesiastes 4:2-3: The dead called better off than the living, and the never-born better than both.
Isaiah 14:9-11: Sheol stirs to meet a fallen king, where maggots are the bedding and worms the blanket.
Job 41:1-11: Leviathan, the creature the day-cursers of 3:8 are said to be able to rouse, described in full.

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as down, dark and silent, with gates and bars. Everyone goes there, king and slave alike, which is exactly Job's point in verses 17 to 19. It is not the same word as Gehenna, the valley outside Jerusalem that gives the New Testament its word for hell; older English versions rendered Sheol as grave, hell and pit in different places, which blurs one Hebrew word into three English ideas.

Job is not naming a pet. He is calling on professional cursers, men paid to lay a spell on a day, and reaching for the most dangerous thing they claim they can stir up. The same creature gets a whole chapter at the end of the book (41:1-34), where the point is that no man can rouse it, hook it or fight it. Balak hiring Balaam in Numbers 22 shows the trade Job is invoking.

The kings Job envies built for permanence and are now under mounds. Ruin fields were visible everywhere in the ancient Near East, since towns were rebuilt on their own rubble until they stood as artificial hills, the tells that archaeologists still dig. Job's argument is that death levels the man who built the tell with the stillborn child of verse 16.

translationNotes.term: Search for it like hidden treasure
translationNotes.note: The verb is the one used for digging out buried valuables. Caches of silver buried in jars under house floors were the normal way to keep wealth safe in a world without banks, and men dug for them in ruins. Job says the miserable dig for death with that same appetite, an image he will pick up again in the mining scene of chapter 28.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job curses the day he was born and wishes he had died in the womb, arguing that death would have brought him peace like the rest and powerful men who have fallen. He questions why God gives life to those in misery and declares that his own life brings only sighing, groaning, and turmoil.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 4
summaryBullets: Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied: (4:1).
“If one ventures a word with you, will you be wearied? Yet who can keep from speaking? (4:2).
Surely you have instructed many, and have strengthened their feeble hands. (4:3).
Your words have steadied those who stumbled; you have braced the knees that were buckling. (4:4).
But now trouble has come upon you, and you are weary. It strikes you, and you are dismayed. (4:5).
Is your reverence not your confidence, and the uprightness of your ways your hope? (4:6).
Consider now, I plead: Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed? (4:7).
As I have observed, those who plow iniquity and those who sow trouble reap the same. (4:8).
By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of His anger they are consumed. (4:9).
The lion may roar, and the fierce lion may growl, yet the teeth of the young lions are broken. (4:10).
The old lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered. (4:11).
Now a word came to me secretly; my ears caught a whisper of it. (4:12).
In disquieting visions in the night, when deep sleep falls on men, (4:13).
fear and trembling came over me and made all my bones shudder. (4:14).
Then a spirit glided past my face, and the hair on my body bristled. (4:15).
It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance; a form loomed before my eyes, and I heard a whispering voice: (4:16).
‘Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker? (4:17).
If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error, (4:18).
how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust, who can be crushed like a moth! (4:19).
They are smashed to pieces from dawn to dusk; unnoticed, they perish forever. (4:20).
Are not their tent cords pulled up, so that they die without wisdom?’ (4:21).
crossRefs: Job 42:7-8: When the LORD finally speaks He addresses Eliphaz the Temanite by name and tells him, 'My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has.'
Galatians 6:7-8: A man reaps what he sows, the proverb Eliphaz is applying at Job 4:8.
Job 15:14-16: Eliphaz repeats the night vision's argument almost word for word in his second speech.
Genesis 15:12: A deep sleep and a dreadful great darkness fall on Abram just before God speaks to him, the same word Eliphaz uses of his night at 4:13.
1 Kings 22:21-22: A spirit comes forward and stands before the LORD in the council and offers to speak, the only other place a spirit steps out like this.

translationNotes.note: A district of Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea, named for a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11,15). It had a standing reputation for wisdom, which is why Jeremiah taunts it: is there no longer any wisdom in Teman (Jeremiah 49:7)? Eliphaz is introduced by that address the way a modern speaker might be introduced by a university. Inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai, written about the eighth century BC, refer to the LORD of Teman.

Not ordinary sleep. This is the heavy trance that falls on a man when God is about to act or speak: on Adam before the woman is made (Genesis 2:21), on Abram at the covenant between the pieces (Genesis 15:12), on Saul's camp when David walks through it (1 Samuel 26:12). Eliphaz uses the word to claim his night experience was a genuine revelation and not a bad dream.

An ordinary house was mud brick on a stone footing, and mud brick dissolves. A wall left unmaintained through two or three wet winters slumps back into the ground it came from, which is why ancient towns rebuilt on their own debris. Eliphaz means the human body, and the picture would land instantly on anyone who had watched an abandoned house melt.

A black goat-hair tent stands only by the tension between its poles and its guy ropes, staked into the ground. Pull the cords and the whole thing collapses at once. It was the standard picture for a life ending suddenly (Isaiah 38:12), and it fits Job, whose household lived in exactly such tents in verse 19 of chapter 1.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: five words in 4:10-11: אַרְיֵה (aryeh), שָׁחַל (shachal), כְּפִיר (kefir), לַיִשׁ (layish), לָבִיא (lavi)
translationNotes.note: Two verses use five different Hebrew words for lion, and English has only the one, so the effect vanishes in translation. Lions lived in the Jordan thickets and the Syrian steppe into historical memory and were hunted by kings from Assyria to Persia; the last lions in the region were shot out during the nineteenth century. Eliphaz is piling up names for the strongest predator anyone knew, to say that even it starves.

translationNotes.term: Who is speaking from here on
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא דִבַּרְתֶּם אֵלַי נְכוֹנָה (lo dibbartem elai nekhonah)
translationNotes.note: This chapter opens the friends' speeches, which fill most of the book. At the end the LORD names Eliphaz the Temanite, the speaker here, and says 'My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has' (Job 42:7). He says it a second time in the next verse and orders seven bulls and seven rams brought so that Job can pray for them (42:8). Lines quoted out of chapters 4 through 25 are the friends talking, and the book records that verdict on them.

stories.keyTakeaway: Eliphaz responds by reminding Job of his past wisdom and suggesting that the innocent do not perish, implying Job must have done wrong; he then recounts a frightening nighttime vision in which a spirit told him that mortals cannot be righteous before God and are fragile creatures who perish without understanding.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 5
summaryBullets: “Call out if you please, but who will answer? To which of the holy ones will you turn? (5:1).
For resentment kills a fool, and envy slays the simple. (5:2).
I have seen a fool taking root, but suddenly his house was cursed. (5:3).
His sons are far from safety, crushed in court without a defender. (5:4).
The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth. (5:5).
For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground. (5:6).
Yet man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward. (5:7).
However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him— (5:8).
the One who does great and unsearchable things, wonders without number. (5:9).
He gives rain to the earth and sends water upon the fields. (5:10).
He sets the lowly on high, so that mourners are lifted to safety. (5:11).
He thwarts the schemes of the crafty, so that their hands find no success. (5:12).
He catches the wise in their craftiness, and sweeps away the plans of the cunning. (5:13).
They encounter darkness by day and grope at noon as in the night. (5:14).
He saves the needy from the sword in their mouth and from the clutches of the powerful. (5:15).
So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth. (5:16).
Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty. (5:17).
For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal. (5:18).
He will rescue you from six calamities; no harm will touch you in seven. (5:19).
In famine He will redeem you from death, and in battle from the stroke of the sword. (5:20).
You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and will not fear havoc when it comes. (5:21).
You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth. (5:22).
For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the wild animals will be at peace with you. (5:23).
You will know that your tent is secure, and find nothing amiss when inspecting your home. (5:24).
You will know that your offspring will be many, your descendants like the grass of the earth. (5:25).
You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season. (5:26).
Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself.” (5:27).
crossRefs: Proverbs 3:11-12: Do not despise the discipline of the LORD, for He corrects the son in whom He delights.
Hebrews 12:5-6: That proverb quoted in full and applied to hardship as a father's training.
1 Corinthians 3:19: Paul quotes Job 5:13 directly, that He catches the wise in their own craftiness.
Deuteronomy 32:39: I wound and I heal, and no one can deliver out of My hand.
Hosea 6:1: He has torn us and He will heal us; He has struck us and He will bind up our wounds.

translationNotes.note: Shaddai is the name for God that runs through this book and almost nowhere else. It occurs about 48 times in the Old Testament and 31 of those are in Job. It is the name God uses with the patriarchs before the name revealed to Moses at the bush (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3), and its heavy use here is one of several marks that put Job's world in the same period as Abraham rather than after Sinai.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַשַּׁעַר (ba-sha'ar), literally in the gate
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew says the sons are crushed in the gate. The gate of a walled town was its courthouse: a deep passage with benches in side chambers where the elders sat, heard cases, witnessed contracts and settled disputes in public. Excavated gates at Dan, Gezer, Megiddo and Beersheba all have these chambers. To be crushed in the gate is to lose a lawsuit with no one to speak for you, which is precisely what Job says he lacks.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּנֵי רֶשֶׁף (bnei reshef), literally sons of the flame
translationNotes.note: The idiom builds a family word: sparks are sons of the fire the way arrows are sons of the quiver (Lamentations 3:13) and a threshing floor's grain is a son of the floor (Isaiah 21:10). Hebrew constantly makes belonging into parentage, and English flattens it. Eliphaz's line is that trouble is as native to man as sparks are to a fire.

translationNotes.term: Covenant with the stones of the field
translationNotes.note: Farming the hill country meant clearing stone before anything could be sown, then clearing it again after every winter's rain lifted more to the surface (Isaiah 5:2). Terrace walls and field cairns across the region are the piles. Eliphaz promises a peace treaty with the one enemy every farmer fought yearly and never beat.

translationNotes.term: Six calamities, no harm in seven
translationNotes.note: A numerical proverb, the pattern of six then seven, three then four, used all through Hebrew wisdom writing (Proverbs 6:16; 30:15-31; Amos 1:3). The second number is the real one and the first sets it up; the form means completeness rather than an exact tally. Eliphaz is saying no disaster of any kind will reach you.

stories.keyTakeaway: Eliphaz warns that resentment destroys the foolish and describes how God overthrows the wicked while lifting the humble; he then urges Job to appeal to God and promises that divine discipline brings healing and protection from calamity.

headings.text: Eliphaz Continues: God Blesses those Who Seek Him

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 6
summaryBullets: Then Job replied: (6:1).
“If only my grief could be weighed and placed with my calamity on the scales. (6:2).
For then it would outweigh the sand of the seas — no wonder my words have been rash. (6:3).
For the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me; my spirit drinks in their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me. (6:4).
Does a wild donkey bray over fresh grass, or an ox low over its fodder? (6:5).
Is tasteless food eaten without salt, or is there flavor in the white of an egg? (6:6).
My soul refuses to touch them; they are loathsome food to me. (6:7).
If only my request were granted and God would fulfill my hope: (6:8).
that God would be willing to crush me, to unleash His hand and cut me off! (6:9).
It still brings me comfort, and joy through unrelenting pain, that I have not denied the words of the Holy One. (6:10).
What strength do I have, that I should still hope? What is my future, that I should be patient? (6:11).
Is my strength like that of stone, or my flesh made of bronze? (6:12).
Is there any help within me now that success is driven from me? (6:13).
A despairing man should have the kindness of his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty. (6:14).
But my brothers are as faithless as wadis, as seasonal streams that overflow, (6:15).
darkened because of the ice and the inflow of melting snow, (6:16).
but ceasing in the dry season and vanishing from their channels in the heat. (6:17).
Caravans turn aside from their routes; they go into the wasteland and perish. (6:18).
The caravans of Tema look for water; the travelers of Sheba hope to find it. (6:19).
They are confounded because they had hoped; their arrival brings disappointment. (6:20).
For now you are of no help; you see terror, and you are afraid. (6:21).
Have I ever said, ‘Give me something; offer me a bribe from your wealth; (6:22).
deliver me from the hand of the enemy; redeem me from the grasp of the ruthless’ ? (6:23).
Teach me, and I will be silent. Help me understand how I have erred. (6:24).
How painful are honest words! But what does your argument prove? (6:25).
Do you intend to correct my words, and treat as wind my cry of despair? (6:26).
You would even cast lots for an orphan and barter away your friend. (6:27).
But now, please look at me. Would I lie to your face? (6:28).
Reconsider; do not be unjust. Reconsider, for my righteousness is at stake. (6:29).
Is there iniquity on my tongue? Can my mouth not discern malice? (6:30).
crossRefs: Isaiah 21:13-15: The caravans of Dedan camp in the scrub and the people of Tema bring water to the thirsty.
Jeremiah 15:18: Will You be to me like a deceptive brook, like waters that fail?
Psalm 38:2: Your arrows have sunk deep into me and Your hand has come down upon me.
Proverbs 17:17: A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Jeremiah 6:16: Ask for the ancient paths, the same road language Job's failed caravans are travelling.

translationNotes.note: A balance with two pans hung from a beam, weighed against carved stone weights. Dozens of Judahite limestone weights survive, dome-shaped and cut with their value; a stone marked beka, found in Jerusalem, weighs 5.71 grams, exactly the half shekel the law required (Exodus 38:26). Job is asking for his grief to be put in one pan against the sand of the sea in the other, which is a merchant's image, not a poet's.

A wadi is a steep dry streambed that runs only in the wet season. In winter it carries meltwater and flash floods and looks like a river; by high summer it is bare gravel. Caravans routed themselves by these beds and died when they arrived to find them empty. That is the whole force of 6:15-20: Job is not saying his friends are unkind, he is saying they are a dry riverbed on the day the water was needed.

A large oasis in northwest Arabia, the modern town of Tayma in Saudi Arabia, and a fixed watering stop on the incense road running north from Yemen. It was important enough that Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, moved his residence there for ten years in the 550s and 540s BC. Isaiah 21:14 and Jeremiah 25:23 both name it. Job is describing traffic on a real trunk route, not wandering nomads.

The Hebrew phrase occurs once in the Bible and its sense is disputed between egg white and the sap of a marsh mallow plant. Either way the point is the same and needs no expertise: it is slime with no taste. Salt was the one seasoning everyone had, cut from the Dead Sea shore, and food without it was the standard byword for the unbearable.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job tells his friends that his suffering is unbearable and he would welcome death; he then accuses them of abandoning him like seasonal streams that dry up, and insists he has done nothing to deserve his fate.

headings.text: Job Replies: My Complaint Is Just

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 7
summaryBullets: “Is not man consigned to labor on earth? Are not his days like those of a hired hand? (7:1).
Like a slave he longs for shade; like a hireling he waits for his wages. (7:2).
So I am allotted months of futility, and nights of misery are appointed to me. (7:3).
When I lie down I think: ‘When will I get up?’ But the night drags on, and I toss and turn until dawn. (7:4).
My flesh is clothed with worms and encrusted with dirt; my skin is cracked and festering. (7:5).
My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle; they come to an end without hope. (7:6).
Remember that my life is but a breath. My eyes will never again see happiness. (7:7).
The eye that beholds me will no longer see me. You will look for me, but I will be no more. (7:8).
As a cloud vanishes and is gone, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come back up. (7:9).
He never returns to his house; his place remembers him no more. (7:10).
Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. (7:11).
Am I the sea, or the monster of the deep, that You must keep me under guard? (7:12).
When I think my bed will comfort me and my couch will ease my complaint, (7:13).
then You frighten me with dreams and terrify me with visions, (7:14).
so that I would prefer strangling and death over my life in this body. (7:15).
I loathe my life! I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath. (7:16).
What is man that You should exalt him, that You should set Your heart upon him, (7:17).
that You attend to him every morning, and test him every moment? (7:18).
Will You never look away from me, or leave me alone to swallow my spittle? (7:19).
If I have sinned, what have I done to You, O watcher of mankind? Why have You made me Your target, so that I am a burden to You? (7:20).
Why do You not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For soon I will lie down in the dust; You will seek me, but I will be no more.” (7:21).
crossRefs: Psalm 8:4: What is man that You are mindful of him, the question Job turns inside out at 7:17.
Deuteronomy 24:14-15: A hired man's pay must be handed over before sunset, because he is counting on it.
Psalm 39:4-6: Let me know how fleeting my life is; every man at his best is but a breath.
2 Samuel 12:23: I will go to him, but he will not return to me.
Job 38:8-11: The LORD answers by asking who shut the sea behind doors and set its bars in place.

translationNotes.note: A day labourer with no land, hired at dawn and paid at dusk, who owned nothing and ate only if he worked. The law required his wage to be paid the same evening because he had no reserve (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15). Job's picture of watching for the shadow to fall is literal: the end of the working day was the moment he got paid and could stop.

Cloth was made on an upright loom with the warp threads hung and tensioned by clay or stone weights, and the weft carried across on a shuttle thrown by hand. Rows of loom weights turn up on the floors of excavated houses. The shuttle crosses in an instant and the thread it lays down runs out; Job is describing both the speed and the ending.

Tannin covers large and dangerous water creatures, and English versions render it sea monster, dragon and serpent in different places (Genesis 1:21; Exodus 7:9-12; Ezekiel 29:3, where Pharaoh is called the great tannin lying in his Nile channels). Job's complaint is sarcastic: Am I the sea itself, or some river beast, that You have to post a guard on me?

An idiom for the smallest possible pause, the space of a swallow. It is still current in Arabic in the same sense. Job is asking for one second of not being watched, and the phrase is deliberately undignified.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job compares human suffering to the misery of slaves and hired workers, describing his own physical torment, sleepless nights, and dread of death; he demands that God stop tormenting him and asks why the Lord examines and tests him so relentlessly instead of forgiving his sins before he dies.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 8
summaryBullets: Then Bildad the Shuhite replied: (8:1).
“How long will you go on saying such things? The words of your mouth are a blustering wind. (8:2).
Does God pervert justice? Does the Almighty pervert what is right? (8:3).
When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion. (8:4).
But if you would earnestly seek God and ask the Almighty for mercy, (8:5).
if you are pure and upright, even now He will rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your righteous estate. (8:6).
Though your beginnings were modest, your latter days will flourish. (8:7).
Please inquire of past generations and consider the discoveries of their fathers. (8:8).
For we were born yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are but a shadow. (8:9).
Will they not teach you and tell you, and speak from their understanding? (8:10).
Does papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Do reeds flourish without water? (8:11).
While the shoots are still uncut, they dry up more quickly than grass. (8:12).
Such is the destiny of all who forget God; so the hope of the godless will perish. (8:13).
His confidence is fragile; his security is in a spider’s web. (8:14).
He leans on his web, but it gives way; he holds fast, but it does not endure. (8:15).
He is a well-watered plant in the sunshine, spreading its shoots over the garden. (8:16).
His roots wrap around the rock heap; he looks for a home among the stones. (8:17).
If he is uprooted from his place, it will disown him, saying, ‘ I never saw you.’ (8:18).
Surely this is the joy of his way; yet others will spring from the dust. (8:19).
Behold, God does not reject the blameless, nor will He strengthen the hand of evildoers. (8:20).
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy. (8:21).
Your enemies will be clothed in shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more.” (8:22).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 32:7: Ask your father and he will tell you, your elders and they will explain it to you.
Psalm 92:12-14: The righteous flourish like a palm and still bear fruit in old age.
Isaiah 59:5-6: The webs of the wicked are no use as clothing and their works do not cover them.
Exodus 2:3: A basket made of papyrus and daubed with tar and pitch, the marsh plant Bildad names at 8:11.
Job 42:7-8: The LORD tells Eliphaz that he and his two friends have not spoken rightly about Him.

translationNotes.note: Bildad is identified by descent from Shuah, a son of Abraham by Keturah who was sent east with his brothers into the country beyond Canaan (Genesis 25:2,6). Assyrian records name a district called Suhu on the middle Euphrates. Either way the friends are all placed in the same arc of desert-edge peoples east and south of Canaan as Job himself.

Papyrus is a tall marsh sedge of the Nile and the Jordan swamps. Egypt cut it for writing sheets, rope, sandals and light river boats, which is the material of the basket that carried the infant Moses (Exodus 2:3) and of the fast skiffs Job names at 9:26. The plant dies fast without standing water, which is Bildad's whole point in verses 11 and 12.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית עַכָּבִישׁ (beit akkavish), literally a spider's house
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew calls it a house, which is the joke: the godless man's security is a house he can put his weight on. Isaiah uses the same picture for work that cannot clothe anyone (Isaiah 59:5-6). Bildad has just told Job that Job's children died for their own sin, so the image of a house that collapses on the people inside it is not idly chosen.

Bildad appeals to inherited wisdom, the sayings of the fathers, which was the recognised authority in a world with almost no books. Israel's law commands the same move (Deuteronomy 32:7), and the wisdom collections of Egypt and Mesopotamia were transmitted as instruction from father to son. Bildad's argument is not private opinion; he is invoking the accepted database.

stories.keyTakeaway: Bildad argues that God does not pervert justice, suggesting Job's children sinned and were punished accordingly; he urges Job to seek God earnestly, promising restoration if he is pure and upright. Bildad illustrates that the godless are fragile like plants without water and spiders' webs, while God will restore the blameless to laughter and shame their enemies.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 9
summaryBullets: Then Job answered: (9:1).
“Yes, I know that it is so, but how can a mortal be righteous before God? (9:2).
If one wished to contend with God, he could not answer Him one time out of a thousand. (9:3).
God is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has resisted Him and prospered? (9:4).
He moves mountains without their knowledge and overturns them in His anger. (9:5).
He shakes the earth from its place, so that its foundations tremble. (9:6).
He commands the sun not to shine; He seals off the stars. (9:7).
He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea. (9:8).
He is the Maker of the Bear and Orion, of the Pleiades and the constellations of the south. (9:9).
He does great things beyond searching out, and wonders without number. (9:10).
Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him; were He to move, I would not recognize Him. (9:11).
If He takes away, who can stop Him? Who dares to ask Him, ‘What are You doing?’ (9:12).
God does not restrain His anger; the helpers of Rahab cower beneath Him. (9:13).
How then can I answer Him or choose my arguments against Him? (9:14).
For even if I were right, I could not answer. I could only beg my Judge for mercy. (9:15).
If I summoned Him and He answered me, I do not believe He would listen to my voice. (9:16).
For He would crush me with a tempest and multiply my wounds without cause. (9:17).
He does not let me catch my breath, but overwhelms me with bitterness. (9:18).
If it is a matter of strength, He is indeed mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon Him? (9:19).
Even if I were righteous, my mouth would condemn me; if I were blameless, it would declare me guilty. (9:20).
Though I am blameless, I have no concern for myself; I despise my own life. (9:21).
It is all the same, and so I say, ‘He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.’ (9:22).
When the scourge brings sudden death, He mocks the despair of the innocent. (9:23).
The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; He blindfolds its judges. If it is not He, then who is it? (9:24).
My days are swifter than a runner; they flee without seeing good. (9:25).
They sweep by like boats of papyrus, like an eagle swooping down on its prey. (9:26).
If I were to say, ‘I will forget my complaint and change my expression and smile,’ (9:27).
I would still dread all my sufferings; I know that You will not acquit me. (9:28).
Since I am already found guilty, why should I labor in vain? (9:29).
If I should wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye, (9:30).
then You would plunge me into the pit, and even my own clothes would despise me. (9:31).
For He is not a man like me, that I can answer Him, that we can take each other to court. (9:32).
Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both. (9:33).
Let Him remove His rod from me, so that His terror will no longer frighten me. (9:34).
Then I would speak without fear of Him. But as it is, I am on my own. (9:35).
crossRefs: Amos 5:8: He who made the Pleiades and Orion and turns deep darkness into morning.
Isaiah 40:22: He stretches out the heavens like a curtain and spreads them like a tent to live in.
1 Timothy 2:5: There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.
Jeremiah 2:22: Though you scrub with lye and use a great deal of soap, your guilt is still a stain before Me.
Job 16:19-21: Job says his witness is in heaven, and wishes a man could argue with God as with a neighbour.

translationNotes.note: Three real star groups, named again at 38:31-32 and paired at Amos 5:8. Kimah is the Pleiades, an open cluster in Taurus about 440 light-years off, of which six or seven show to the naked eye. Kesil is Orion, and the Hebrew word means fool or dullard, a sense the English name loses completely. Ash is the group English calls the Bear or the Plough. The chambers of the south are the constellations that rise only low on the southern horizon from that latitude.

Not a counsellor and not a comforter. A mokhiach is an arbitrator with authority to decide between two parties and enforce it, from a root meaning to adjudicate. The phrase lay his hand on us both is the gesture of a man with jurisdiction over both sides. Job's problem is procedural: in every ordinary lawsuit you go up to a higher court, and here the other party is the court.

Reed skiffs, bundles of papyrus lashed into a hull, light enough for two men to carry and very fast on the Nile. Isaiah pictures envoys sent in exactly these vessels (Isaiah 18:2). Job stacks three speeds in three lines: a running courier, a reed boat, a diving eagle. All three were the fastest things anyone in that world had seen.

Two cleaning agents. Bor is a potash lye made by leaching wood ash through water, harsh enough to strip grease. Neter is natron, a natural soda mined from dry lake beds in Egypt, the same substance the Egyptians used to dry bodies. Jeremiah pairs them for the same argument (Jeremiah 2:22). Job means the strongest scouring known, and says it would not help.

A name for a proud power of the sea that God subdues, used again at 26:12. Elsewhere Scripture applies it as a byname for Egypt: Isaiah calls Egypt Rahab who sits still (Isaiah 30:7), and Psalm 87:4 lists Rahab beside Babylon. It is not the Rahab of Jericho, which is a different Hebrew name with a different spelling.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job acknowledges God's vast power and wisdom, then argues that mortals cannot dispute with him or prove their innocence, since God crushes the blameless and wicked alike without restraint. Job expresses despair that no mediator exists between himself and God, leaving him unable to speak freely in his own defense.

headings.text: Job: How Can I Contend with God?

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 10
summaryBullets: “I loathe my own life; I will express my complaint and speak in the bitterness of my soul. (10:1).
I will say to God: Do not condemn me! Let me know why You prosecute me. (10:2).
Does it please You to oppress me, to reject the work of Your hands and favor the schemes of the wicked? (10:3).
Do You have eyes of flesh? Do You see as man sees? (10:4).
Are Your days like those of a mortal, or Your years like those of a man, (10:5).
that You should seek my iniquity and search out my sin — (10:6).
though You know that I am not guilty, and there is no deliverance from Your hand? (10:7).
Your hands shaped me and altogether formed me. Would You now turn and destroy me? (10:8).
Please remember that You molded me like clay. Would You now return me to dust? (10:9).
Did You not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese? (10:10).
You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. (10:11).
You have granted me life and loving devotion, and Your care has preserved my spirit. (10:12).
Yet You concealed these things in Your heart, and I know that this was in Your mind: (10:13).
If I sinned, You would take note, and would not acquit me of my iniquity. (10:14).
If I am guilty, woe to me! And even if I am righteous, I cannot lift my head. I am full of shame and aware of my affliction. (10:15).
Should I hold my head high, You would hunt me like a lion, and again display Your power against me. (10:16).
You produce new witnesses against me and multiply Your anger toward me. Hardships assault me in wave after wave. (10:17).
Why then did You bring me from the womb? Oh, that I had died, and no eye had seen me! (10:18).
If only I had never come to be, but had been carried from the womb to the grave. (10:19).
Are my days not few? Withdraw from me, that I may have a little comfort, (10:20).
before I go — never to return — to a land of darkness and gloom, (10:21).
to a land of utter darkness, of deep shadow and disorder, where even the light is like darkness.” (10:22).
crossRefs: Psalm 139:13-16: You knit me together in my mother's womb and Your eyes saw my unformed body.
Isaiah 64:8: We are the clay and You are the potter; we are all the work of Your hand.
Genesis 2:7: The LORD God forms the man from the dust of the ground and breathes into his nostrils.
Psalm 88:10-12: Are Your wonders known in the dark, or Your righteousness in the land of forgetting?
Job 33:6: Elihu answers Job's clay image by saying that he too was pinched off from clay.

translationNotes.note: Riv is the standard word for a lawsuit, the whole legal dispute, and it runs under this book from beginning to end. Job is not asking why he feels bad; he is demanding the charge sheet, the way a defendant demands to know the indictment. Verse 2 is literally: tell me what You are contending with me about.

translationNotes.term: Poured out like milk, curdled like cheese
translationNotes.note: A dairy image from ordinary work: milk poured from a skin and set with rennet until it firms into curd. Cheese-making was daily labour in a herding household, and Job uses it for the formation of a body in the womb, liquid becoming solid. It is a kitchen picture, not a delicate one, and that is deliberate.

The potter kneaded clay by hand, threw it, and if the vessel went wrong crushed it back into a lump and started again. The prophets use the same workshop for the same argument (Isaiah 64:8; Jeremiah 18:1-6). Job's complaint has teeth precisely because a potter is free to do that, and he is asking whether God intends to.

translationNotes.term: A land of darkness and gloom
translationNotes.note: The word behind shadow of death in older English, also rendered deep darkness. It is used of a mine shaft at 28:3, of the deepest night at 24:17, and famously of the valley in Psalm 23:4. Job's closing line stacks the darkest words Hebrew has, ending with a phrase that says even the light there is like darkness.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job tells God he loathes his life and demands to know what charges God has against him, arguing that God shaped him in the womb yet now pursues him relentlessly like a lion. He wishes he had died at birth and begs God to leave him alone before he descends into darkness and the grave.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 11
summaryBullets: Then Zophar the Naamathite replied: (11:1).
“Should this stream of words go unanswered and such a speaker be vindicated? (11:2).
Should your babbling put others to silence? Will you scoff without rebuke? (11:3).
You have said, ‘My doctrine is sound, and I am pure in Your sight.’ (11:4).
But if only God would speak and open His lips against you, (11:5).
and disclose to you the secrets of wisdom, for true wisdom has two sides. Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves. (11:6).
Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty? (11:7).
They are higher than the heavens— what can you do? They are deeper than Sheol— what can you know? (11:8).
Their measure is longer than the earth and wider than the sea. (11:9).
If He comes along to imprison you, or convenes a court, who can stop Him? (11:10).
Surely He knows the deceit of men. If He sees iniquity, does He not take note? (11:11).
But a witless man can no more become wise than the colt of a wild donkey can be born a man! (11:12).
As for you, if you direct your heart and lift up your hands to Him, (11:13).
if you put away the iniquity in your hand, and allow no injustice to dwell in your tents, (11:14).
then indeed you will lift up your face without blemish; you will stand firm and unafraid. (11:15).
For you will forget your misery, recalling it only as waters gone by. (11:16).
Your life will be brighter than noonday; its darkness will be like the morning. (11:17).
You will be secure, because there is hope, and you will look around and lie down in safety. (11:18).
You will lie down without fear, and many will court your favor. (11:19).
But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and escape will elude them; they will hope for their last breath.” (11:20).
crossRefs: Isaiah 55:8-9: My thoughts are not your thoughts, and My ways are higher than your ways.
Romans 11:33-34: The depth of God's wisdom and knowledge, and who has ever known the mind of the Lord.
Psalm 139:7-10: If I go up to the heavens You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there.
Ezra 9:13: You, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved.
Job 42:9: Zophar the Naamathite named among the three who must bring an offering and be prayed for.

translationNotes.note: Zophar's home is the one of the four that cannot be fixed on a map. A town called Naamah appears in the Judean lowlands (Joshua 15:41), but that is well inside Canaan and does not fit a book set among the peoples of the east. The honest position is that the place is named and its site is not established.

translationNotes.term: Higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol
translationNotes.note: Zophar measures God's wisdom by the four dimensions the ancient world used: up to the sky, down to the realm of the dead, long as the earth, wide as the sea (11:8-9). The same four-way sweep appears in Psalm 139:8-9 and in Paul's prayer at Ephesians 3:18. It is the standard Hebrew way of saying every direction there is.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּרַשׂ כַּף (paras kaf), to spread the palm
translationNotes.note: The normal posture of prayer was standing with both hands open and raised, palms up, not folded and not kneeling. Solomon prays that way at the temple dedication (1 Kings 8:22), and Paul assumes it still (1 Timothy 2:8). Zophar is telling Job to adopt the physical stance of a petitioner who has dropped his case.

translationNotes.term: The colt of a wild donkey
translationNotes.note: The onager, the wild ass of the Syrian and Arabian steppe, was proverbially untameable and outside all human control; God Himself takes up the same animal at 39:5-8. Domestic donkeys carried everything; the wild kind carried nothing and could not be broken. Zophar's insult in verse 12 is that a stupid man will get sense about the day one of those is born human.

stories.keyTakeaway: Zophar rebukes Job for his words, insists God's wisdom is incomprehensible, and argues that if Job would turn from sin and devote himself to God, he would be restored to prosperity and security.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 12
summaryBullets: Then Job answered: (12:1).
“Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die! (12:2).
But I also have a mind; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these? (12:3).
I am a laughingstock to my friends, though I called on God, and He answered. The righteous and upright man is a laughingstock. (12:4).
The one at ease scorns misfortune as the fate of those whose feet are slipping. (12:5).
The tents of robbers are safe, and those who provoke God are secure — those who carry their god in their hands. (12:6).
But ask the animals, and they will instruct you; ask the birds of the air, and they will tell you. (12:7).
Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you; let the fish of the sea inform you. (12:8).
Which of all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this? (12:9).
The life of every living thing is in His hand, as well as the breath of all mankind. (12:10).
Does not the ear test words as the tongue tastes its food? (12:11).
Wisdom is found with the elderly, and understanding comes with long life. (12:12).
Wisdom and strength belong to God; counsel and understanding are His. (12:13).
What He tears down cannot be rebuilt; the man He imprisons cannot be released. (12:14).
If He holds back the waters, they dry up, and if He releases them, they overwhelm the land. (12:15).
True wisdom and power belong to Him. The deceived and the deceiver are His. (12:16).
He leads counselors away barefoot and makes fools of judges. (12:17).
He loosens the bonds placed by kings and fastens a belt around their waists. (12:18).
He leads priests away barefoot and overthrows the established. (12:19).
He deprives the trusted of speech and takes away the discernment of elders. (12:20).
He pours out contempt on nobles and disarms the mighty. (12:21).
He reveals the deep things of darkness and brings deep shadows into light. (12:22).
He makes nations great and destroys them; He enlarges nations, then disperses them. (12:23).
He deprives the earth’s leaders of reason and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland. (12:24).
They grope in the darkness without light; He makes them stagger like drunkards. (12:25).
crossRefs: Proverbs 6:6: Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider her ways and be wise.
Isaiah 40:23: He reduces rulers to nothing and makes the judges of the earth as emptiness.
Daniel 2:20-22: He changes times and seasons, removes kings and sets up kings, and reveals deep things.
Psalm 107:40: He pours contempt on nobles and makes them wander in a trackless waste.
Isaiah 20:2-4: Captives led away stripped and barefoot, the picture behind Job 12:17-19.

translationNotes.note: Prisoners of war were driven away stripped and unshod, and Assyrian palace reliefs show exactly that: lines of captives barefoot, with their possessions on their backs. Isaiah is ordered to walk naked and barefoot for three years as a sign of it (Isaiah 20:2-4). Job is not describing men who have lost an argument; he is describing men in a deportation column.

translationNotes.term: Fastens a belt around their waists
translationNotes.note: The line is a reversal in two halves: God loosens the belt kings wear as the badge of command, then ties a rope round their own waists as prisoners. The waistband held the sword and marked rank, so to be ungirded was to be disarmed and demoted. Jeremiah is sent to bury a linen ezor to make the same point about Judah (Jeremiah 13:1-11).

Job answers the friends' appeal to inherited human wisdom by sending them to livestock, birds, the ground and fish. It is an argument by insult: what you are telling me is so obvious that the cattle know it. The four categories match the order of creatures in Genesis 1, and the LORD will pick up exactly this method in chapters 38 to 41, running Job through the animal world one species at a time.

translationNotes.term: Carry their god in their hands
translationNotes.note: Portable idols, small enough to hold. Rachel steals her father's household gods and sits on them in a camel saddle (Genesis 31:19,34), and Isaiah mocks gods that have to be loaded onto pack animals when the city falls (Isaiah 46:1-2). Job's dig is that the men who are safest are the ones whose god fits in a fist.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job tells his friends they have no monopoly on wisdom, then catalogs God's absolute power over all creation - he tears down and rebuilds, controls water and drought, strips rulers of authority, and confounds the mighty and the wise alike.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 13
summaryBullets: “Indeed, my eyes have seen all this; my ears have heard and understood. (13:1).
What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you. (13:2).
Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and argue my case before God. (13:3).
You, however, smear with lies; you are all worthless physicians. (13:4).
If only you would remain silent; for that would be your wisdom! (13:5).
Hear now my argument, and listen to the plea of my lips. (13:6).
Will you speak wickedly on God’s behalf or speak deceitfully for Him? (13:7).
Would you show Him partiality or argue in His defense? (13:8).
Would it be well when He examined you? Could you deceive Him as you would deceive a man? (13:9).
Surely He would rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality. (13:10).
Would His majesty not terrify you? Would the dread of Him not fall upon you? (13:11).
Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay. (13:12).
Be silent, and I will speak. Then let come to me what may. (13:13).
Why do I put myself at risk and take my life in my own hands? (13:14).
Though He slay me, I will hope in Him. I will still defend my ways to His face. (13:15).
Moreover, this will be my salvation, for no godless man can appear before Him. (13:16).
Listen carefully to my words; let my declaration ring in your ears. (13:17).
See now, I have prepared my case; I know that I will be vindicated. (13:18).
Can anyone indict me? If so, I will be silent and die. (13:19).
Only grant these two things to me, so that I need not hide from You: (13:20).
Withdraw Your hand from me, and do not let Your terror frighten me. (13:21).
Then call me, and I will answer, or let me speak, and You can reply. (13:22).
How many are my iniquities and sins? Reveal to me my transgression and sin. (13:23).
Why do You hide Your face and consider me as Your enemy? (13:24).
Would You frighten a windblown leaf? Would You chase after dry chaff? (13:25).
For You record bitter accusations against me and bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth. (13:26).
You put my feet in the stocks and stand watch over all my paths; You set a limit for the soles of my feet. (13:27).
So man wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment. (13:28).
crossRefs: Isaiah 1:18: Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD, the same courtroom summons Job wants.
Jeremiah 20:2: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks at the upper Benjamin Gate.
Acts 16:24: The jailer at Philippi fastens Paul and Silas in the stocks in the inner cell.
Psalm 44:24: Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?
Job 9:32-35: Job's earlier complaint that there is no arbiter to lay a hand on him and on God together.

translationNotes.note: The chapter is built out of courtroom vocabulary: prepare a case (13:18), be vindicated or declared in the right, bring an indictment (13:19), summon and answer (13:22). Job is not venting. He is filing, and the technical terms are the same ones used for a suit heard by elders in the town gate.

Elil means a nothing, and it is the word the prophets use for idols (Leviticus 19:4; Isaiah 2:8). Ancient medicine was mostly bandaging, oil, wine, splints and herbs, so a doctor who smeared on a useless plaster was a known figure of contempt. Job calls his friends quacks who plaster over the problem with lies.

translationNotes.term: Take my life in my own hands
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָשִׂים נַפְשִׁי בְּכַפִּי (asim nafshi be-khappi)
translationNotes.note: A set idiom for deliberately risking death, used of soldiers and of people acting against a king's power (Judges 12:3; 1 Samuel 19:5; 1 Samuel 28:21). It is the ancestor of the English phrase, and here it means Job knows that pressing this suit could kill him and is doing it anyway.

A split timber that clamped the ankles and held a prisoner sitting, forcing the legs apart. It punished by exposure and cramp as much as by confinement, and it was set up in public. Jeremiah spends a night in one at a temple gate (Jeremiah 20:2), and Paul and Silas are locked in one at Philippi (Acts 16:24). Elihu quotes this same complaint of Job's back at him at 33:11.

Cloth was expensive, made by hand from fleece or flax, and a good garment was inherited property that could be seized as security for a loan (Exodus 22:26). Clothes moths ate it invisibly in storage. The image is of wealth that disappears without anyone touching it, and Isaiah and Hosea both use the same insect the same way (Isaiah 50:9; Hosea 5:12).

stories.keyTakeaway: Job dismisses his friends as worthless physicians and declares he will argue his case directly with God, saying he will defend his ways even if God slays him. He then appeals to God to remove his terror and reveal what wrongs he has committed, asking why God treats him as an enemy.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 14
summaryBullets: “Man, who is born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble. (14:1).
Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure. (14:2).
Do You open Your eyes to one like this? Will You bring him into judgment before You? (14:3).
Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one! (14:4).
Since his days are determined and the number of his months is with You, and since You have set limits that he cannot exceed, (14:5).
look away from him and let him rest, so he can enjoy his day as a hired hand. (14:6).
For there is hope for a tree: If it is cut down, it will sprout again, and its tender shoots will not fail. (14:7).
If its roots grow old in the ground and its stump dies in the soil, (14:8).
at the scent of water it will bud and put forth twigs like a sapling. (14:9).
But a man dies and is laid low; he breathes his last, and where is he? (14:10).
As water disappears from the sea and a river becomes parched and dry, (14:11).
so a man lies down and does not rise. Until the heavens are no more, he will not be awakened or roused from sleep. (14:12).
If only You would hide me in Sheol and conceal me until Your anger has passed! If only You would appoint a time for me and then remember me! (14:13).
When a man dies, will he live again? All the days of my hard service I will wait, until my renewal comes. (14:14).
You will call, and I will answer; You will desire the work of Your hands. (14:15).
For then You would count my steps, but would not keep track of my sin. (14:16).
My transgression would be sealed in a bag, and You would cover over my iniquity. (14:17).
But as a mountain erodes and crumbles and a rock is dislodged from its place, (14:18).
as water wears away the stones and torrents wash away the soil, so You destroy a man’s hope. (14:19).
You forever overpower him, and he passes on; You change his countenance and send him away. (14:20).
If his sons receive honor, he does not know it; if they are brought low, he is unaware. (14:21).
He feels only the pain of his own body and mourns only for himself.” (14:22).
crossRefs: Psalm 103:15-16: Man's days are like grass; the wind passes over it and its place knows it no more.
Isaiah 6:13: A stump is left when the terebinth is felled, and that stump is the holy seed.
Daniel 12:2: Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to life everlasting.
1 Samuel 25:29: The life of my lord will be bound up in the bundle of the living with the LORD your God.
Job 19:25-27: Job's later declaration that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God with his own eyes.

translationNotes.note: Not poetry but arboriculture. Olives, figs, terebinths and oaks all regrow from the cut stump, and an olive coppiced at ground level will throw new shoots and bear again; groves in the region are still worked that way. Job's contrast in verses 7 to 12 is between a stump that answers to the smell of water and a man who does not. Isaiah takes the same fact and turns it the other way (Isaiah 6:13).

Valuables, silver, and legal tokens were carried in a small pouch tied shut and stamped with a seal so the knot could not be opened undetected. Clay seal impressions from such closures survive in the hundreds. Job pictures his own offences bagged, sealed and set aside rather than read out in court, which is the opposite of the indictment he demands in chapter 31.

The noun means a change or a relief, and it is used for a change of clothes (Genesis 45:22) and for a shift of workers rotating off duty (1 Kings 5:14, where Solomon's levy served in Lebanon a month at a time). Job has already called life hard service, so the word means the end of his shift, the moment the relief crew arrives.

translationNotes.term: As water wears away the stones
translationNotes.note: Limestone is the bedrock of the whole region, and running water cuts it visibly: the wadis are gorges, and every winter's flood moves rock and strips soil off the slopes. Job's four images in verses 18 and 19 are all real erosion he had watched, stacked to say that the process is slow, total and irreversible, and that God does the same to a man's hope.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job describes human life as brief and troubled, comparing mortals to flowers that wither; he then laments that unlike trees, humans do not return after death, though he expresses a faint hope that God might hide him in the grave and eventually restore him.

headings.text: Job Laments the Finality of Death

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 15
summaryBullets: Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied: (15:1).
“Does a wise man answer with empty counsel or fill his belly with the hot east wind? (15:2).
Should he argue with useless words or speeches that serve no purpose? (15:3).
But you even undermine the fear of God and hinder meditation before Him. (15:4).
For your iniquity instructs your mouth, and you choose the language of the crafty. (15:5).
Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you. (15:6).
Were you the first man ever born? Were you brought forth before the hills? (15:7).
Do you listen in on the council of God or limit wisdom to yourself? (15:8).
What do you know that we do not? What do you understand that is not clear to us? (15:9).
Both the gray-haired and the aged are on our side — men much older than your father. (15:10).
Are the consolations of God not enough for you, even words spoken gently to you? (15:11).
Why has your heart carried you away, and why do your eyes flash, (15:12).
so that you turn your spirit against God and pour such words from your mouth? (15:13).
What is man, that he should be pure, or one born of woman, that he should be righteous? (15:14).
If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes, (15:15).
how much less man, who is vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water? (15:16).
Listen to me and I will inform you. I will describe what I have seen, (15:17).
what was declared by wise men and was not concealed from their fathers, (15:18).
to whom alone the land was given when no foreigner passed among them. (15:19).
A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless. (15:20).
Sounds of terror fill his ears; in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him. (15:21).
He despairs of his return from darkness; he is marked for the sword. (15:22).
He wanders about as food for vultures; he knows the day of darkness is at hand. (15:23).
Distress and anguish terrify him, overwhelming him like a king poised to attack. (15:24).
For he has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty, (15:25).
rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield. (15:26).
Though his face is covered with fat and his waistline bulges with flesh, (15:27).
he will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble. (15:28).
He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure. His possessions will not overspread the land. (15:29).
He will not escape from the darkness; the flame will wither his shoots, and the breath of God’s mouth will carry him away. (15:30).
Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness, for emptiness will be his reward. (15:31).
It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not flourish. (15:32).
He will be like a vine stripped of its unripe grapes, like an olive tree that sheds its blossoms. (15:33).
For the company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery. (15:34).
They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit.” (15:35).
crossRefs: Job 4:12-21: Eliphaz's first speech, where this same argument arrived as a night vision.
Proverbs 8:22-25: Wisdom speaks of being brought forth before the hills, the claim Eliphaz mocks at 15:7.
Psalm 73:3-12: Asaph looks hard at the prosperity of the wicked before he reconsiders it.
Job 21:7-13: Job's direct answer, that the wicked often grow old, grow powerful and die at ease.
Genesis 3:19: You are dust, and to dust you will return.

translationNotes.note: A real and dreaded wind, the sirocco, which blows off the Arabian desert in spring and autumn. It raises the temperature sharply in hours, carries dust, withers standing crops and makes people ill-tempered and unable to work. Scripture uses it for the blasting of grain (Genesis 41:6), for the wind that dries the sea (Exodus 14:21) and for the one that beats on Jonah's head (Jonah 4:8). Eliphaz accuses Job of filling his belly with it: hot, dry and destructive.

Sod means the closed circle where decisions are made before they are announced, and by extension the secret business of that circle. Jeremiah says the false prophets never stood in the LORD's sod (Jeremiah 23:18,22), and Amos says God does nothing without revealing His sod to His servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). Eliphaz's sneer is precise: have you been in the room?

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גַּב מָגִנָּיו (gav maginnav), the boss of his shields
translationNotes.note: A large shield was wood and hide with a raised metal boss at the centre. A man charged behind it with the boss forward, using it as a battering surface, not merely as cover. Eliphaz pictures the wicked man running at God shield-first, which is a battlefield image of deliberate assault rather than defence.

In a world where most people were thin because most people were hungry, body fat read as wealth, not as ill health. The idiom is used for arrogance and insensitivity throughout the Old Testament: their heart is fat as grease (Psalm 119:70), and Jeshurun grew fat and kicked (Deuteronomy 32:15). Eliphaz is describing a rich man's complacency, not his waistline.

stories.keyTakeaway: Eliphaz accuses Job of impiety and argues that mortals cannot be righteous before God; he then describes the suffering that awaits the wicked man, saying Job's words reveal his guilt.

headings.text: Eliphaz: Job Does Not Fear God

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 16
summaryBullets: Then Job answered: (16:1).
“I have heard many things like these; miserable comforters are you all. (16:2).
Is there no end to your long-winded speeches? What provokes you to continue testifying? (16:3).
I could also speak like you if you were in my place; I could heap up words against you and shake my head at you. (16:4).
But I would encourage you with my mouth, and the consolation of my lips would bring relief. (16:5).
Even if I speak, my pain is not relieved, and if I hold back, how will it go away? (16:6).
Surely He has now exhausted me; You have devastated all my family. (16:7).
You have bound me, and it has become a witness; my frailty rises up and testifies against me. (16:8).
His anger has torn me and opposed me; He gnashes His teeth at me. My adversary pierces me with His eyes. (16:9).
They open their mouths against me and strike my cheeks with contempt; they join together against me. (16:10).
God has delivered me to unjust men; He has thrown me to the clutches of the wicked. (16:11).
I was at ease, but He shattered me; He seized me by the neck and crushed me. He has set me up as His target; (16:12).
His archers surround me. He pierces my kidneys without mercy and spills my gall on the ground. (16:13).
He breaks me with wound upon wound; He rushes me like a mighty warrior. (16:14).
I have sewn sackcloth over my skin; I have buried my horn in the dust. (16:15).
My face is red with weeping, and deep shadows ring my eyes; (16:16).
yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure. (16:17).
O earth, do not cover my blood; may my cry for help never be laid to rest. (16:18).
Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high. (16:19).
My friends are my scoffers as my eyes pour out tears to God. (16:20).
Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor! (16:21).
For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return. (16:22).
crossRefs: Job 13:4: Job's earlier verdict on the same men, that they are plasterers of lies and worthless physicians.
Genesis 31:47-50: Laban names the heap in Aramaic and calls on God as the witness between the two parties.
Psalm 22:12-13: Bulls of Bashan encircle me and open their mouths wide against me.
Genesis 4:10: Your brother's blood is crying out to Me from the ground.
1 John 2:1: We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.

translationNotes.note: The verse uses two words for witness, and the second one, sahed, is Aramaic, not Hebrew. It appears nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Its only relative in Scripture is the Aramaic name Laban gives the covenant heap, Jegar-sahadutha, the heap of witness (Genesis 31:47). Job is reaching outside his own language for the technical term: he wants a sworn witness on the stand who can testify to what he actually did.

Coarse cloth woven from black goat hair, the same material tents and grain sacks were made of, worn next to the skin so it scratched. It was the standard dress of mourning and repentance across the region (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5-8; Matthew 11:21). Job says he has sewn it onto his skin, which is stronger than wearing it: he is not putting on a garment he can take off.

translationNotes.term: Buried my horn in the dust
translationNotes.note: The horn of a bull or ram stands for strength and standing, so to have your horn lifted is to be honoured (1 Samuel 2:1; Psalm 92:10) and to have it cut off is to be ruined (Lamentations 2:3). Job says he has pushed his own horn into the dirt. English keeps the word and loses the meaning entirely.

Unburied blood was held to cry out until the case was answered, which is the argument in Genesis 4:10-11 and the reason the law required spilled blood to be covered with earth (Leviticus 17:13). Job asks the earth to leave his blood exposed on the surface so that his case cannot be quietly closed. It is a legal request, not a curse.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job rebukes his friends as miserable comforters, then describes God assailing him with relentless cruelty while people mock and strike him; despite his physical devastation and weeping, he insists his hands are free of violence and declares that his witness and advocate remain in heaven.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 17
summaryBullets: “My spirit is broken; my days are extinguished; the grave awaits me. (17:1).
Surely mockers surround me, and my eyes must gaze at their rebellion. (17:2).
Give me, I pray, the pledge You demand. Who else will be my guarantor? (17:3).
You have closed their minds to understanding; therefore You will not exalt them. (17:4).
If a man denounces his friends for a price, the eyes of his children will fail. (17:5).
He has made me a byword among the people, a man in whose face they spit. (17:6).
My eyes have grown dim with grief, and my whole body is but a shadow. (17:7).
The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent are stirred against the godless. (17:8).
Yet a righteous one holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger. (17:9).
But come back and try again, all of you. For I will not find a wise man among you. (17:10).
My days have passed; my plans are broken off — even the desires of my heart. (17:11).
They have turned night into day, making light seem near in the face of darkness. (17:12).
If I look for Sheol as my home, if I spread out my bed in darkness, (17:13).
and say to corruption, ‘You are my father,’ and to the worm, ‘My mother,’ or ‘My sister,’ (17:14).
where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me? (17:15).
Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?” (17:16).
crossRefs: Job 30:9: Job repeats the charge that he has become their drinking song and their byword.
Psalm 44:14: You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.
Proverbs 6:1-5: The warning about striking hands as surety for another man, the pledge Job asks God to give.
Isaiah 38:10: In the prime of my life I must pass through the gates of Sheol and be robbed of my years.
