Psalm 88:18: You have taken from me friend and neighbour; the darkness is my closest companion.

translationNotes.note: In an ordinary loan a third party pledged himself for the debtor, striking hands on it, and was liable if the debtor defaulted (Proverbs 6:1-2; 17:18). Judah offers himself as surety for Benjamin in exactly this sense (Genesis 43:9). Job asks God to post the bond for him, because there is no one else solvent enough to guarantee his appearance in a case against God.

A mashal is a proverb or a saying, and to become one is to have your name turned into a general term for disaster, used by people who never met you. Israel is warned of the same fate (Deuteronomy 28:37; 1 Kings 9:7). Job is complaining about reputation as a permanent public object, which is why he wants a written record in 19:23-24.

translationNotes.term: A man in whose face they spit
translationNotes.note: Spitting in the face was formal public disgrace, not a loss of temper. It shames Miriam for seven days by comparison (Numbers 12:14), and it is the prescribed act of a widow whose brother-in-law refuses to marry her (Deuteronomy 25:9). Isaiah's servant does not hide his face from it (Isaiah 50:6). Job means he has been ritually degraded, not merely insulted.

translationNotes.term: You are my father, my mother, my sister
translationNotes.note: Job takes the words a man says over his own kin and gives them to the pit and the maggot. In a society where identity was family, saying this to corruption and the worm is the total loss of household, which is what chapter 19 spells out person by person. It is a formal address, not a poetic flourish.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job declares his spirit broken and his days numbered, insisting God alone can vouch for him while his friends mock him and the righteous watch in horror. He sees death approaching, finds his plans destroyed, and questions whether any hope remains for him.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 18
summaryBullets: Then Bildad the Shuhite replied: (18:1).
“How long until you end these speeches? Show some sense, and then we can talk. (18:2).
Why are we regarded as cattle, as stupid in your sight? (18:3).
You who tear yourself in anger— should the earth be forsaken on your account, or the rocks be moved from their place? (18:4).
Indeed, the lamp of the wicked is extinguished; the flame of his fire does not glow. (18:5).
The light in his tent grows dark, and the lamp beside him goes out. (18:6).
His vigorous stride is shortened, and his own schemes trip him up. (18:7).
For his own feet lead him into a net, and he wanders into its mesh. (18:8).
A trap seizes his heel; a snare grips him. (18:9).
A noose is hidden in the ground, and a trap lies in his path. (18:10).
Terrors frighten him on every side and harass his every step. (18:11).
His strength is depleted, and calamity is ready at his side. (18:12).
It devours patches of his skin; the firstborn of death devours his limbs. (18:13).
He is torn from the shelter of his tent and is marched off to the king of terrors. (18:14).
Fire resides in his tent; burning sulfur rains down on his dwelling. (18:15).
The roots beneath him dry up, and the branches above him wither away. (18:16).
The memory of him perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the land. (18:17).
He is driven from light into darkness and is chased from the inhabited world. (18:18).
He has no offspring or posterity among his people, no survivor where he once lived. (18:19).
Those in the west are appalled at his fate, while those in the east tremble in horror. (18:20).
Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God.” (18:21).
crossRefs: Proverbs 13:9: The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is snuffed out.
Proverbs 24:20: The evil man has no future, and the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished.
Psalm 9:15-16: The nations have fallen into the pit they dug; their feet are caught in the net they hid.
Deuteronomy 29:20: The LORD blots out his name from under heaven.
Job 21:17: Job asks straight out how often the lamp of the wicked is actually put out.

translationNotes.note: A household lamp was a shallow clay saucer with a pinched lip holding a flax wick in olive oil, and it was kept burning through the night in an occupied house. A dark house meant an empty house or a dead family, and the same image stands for a surviving heir, as when God promises David a lamp in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36). Bildad's six words for light going out in verses 5 and 6 mean extinction of the line, not gloom.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֶשֶׁת (reshet), שְׂבָכָה (sevakhah), פַּח (pach), צַמִּים (tsammim), חֶבֶל (chevel), מַלְכֹּדֶת (malkodet)
translationNotes.note: Verses 8 to 10 name six distinct pieces of hunting gear: a net, a mesh, a spring trap, a snare, a hidden rope and a deadfall. English blurs them into net, trap and snare, so the relentlessness of the list is lost. Hunters took birds and gazelle with exactly this equipment, and Bildad is describing a man walking into a laid-out trapline where every device is already set.

Hebrew names a thing's most extreme instance as its firstborn, the way the poorest of the poor are called the firstborn of the poor (Isaiah 14:30). So the firstborn of death is the deadliest disease death has, eating the man's skin and limbs by pieces. Bildad says this to a man covered in sores, which is not an accident.

Death pictured as a sovereign who has his subjects marched to him under escort. The surrounding peoples had named death-gods with courts and gates, and Scripture uses the same royal imagery while giving death no name of its own here. The phrase occurs once in the Bible and it is the strongest personification of death in the Old Testament.

stories.keyTakeaway: Bildad rebukes Job for his complaints and delivers an extended description of how the wicked are destroyed - trapped, terrified, consumed by calamity, and utterly erased from memory and the earth.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 19
summaryBullets: Then Job answered: (19:1).
“How long will you torment me and crush me with your words? (19:2).
Ten times now you have reproached me; you shamelessly mistreat me. (19:3).
Even if I have truly gone astray, my error concerns me alone. (19:4).
If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me and use my disgrace against me, (19:5).
then understand that it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me. (19:6).
Though I cry out, ‘Violence!’ I get no response; though I call for help, there is no justice. (19:7).
He has blocked my way so I cannot pass; He has veiled my paths with darkness. (19:8).
He has stripped me of my honor and removed the crown from my head. (19:9).
He tears me down on every side until I am gone; He uproots my hope like a tree. (19:10).
His anger burns against me, and He counts me among His enemies. (19:11).
His troops advance together; they construct a ramp against me and encamp around my tent. (19:12).
He has removed my brothers from me; my acquaintances have abandoned me. (19:13).
My kinsmen have failed me, and my friends have forgotten me. (19:14).
My guests and maidservants count me as a stranger; I am a foreigner in their sight. (19:15).
I call for my servant, but he does not answer, though I implore him with my own mouth. (19:16).
My breath is repulsive to my wife, and I am loathsome to my own family. (19:17).
Even little boys scorn me; when I appear, they deride me. (19:18).
All my best friends despise me, and those I love have turned against me. (19:19).
My skin and flesh cling to my bones; I have escaped by the skin of my teeth. (19:20).
Have pity on me, my friends, have pity, for the hand of God has struck me. (19:21).
Why do you persecute me as God does? Will you never get enough of my flesh? (19:22).
I wish that my words were recorded and inscribed in a book, (19:23).
by an iron stylus on lead, or chiseled in stone forever. (19:24).
But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth. (19:25).
Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God. (19:26).
I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger. How my heart yearns within me! (19:27).
If you say, ‘Let us persecute him, since the root of the matter lies with him,’ (19:28).
then you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword, so that you may know there is a judgment.” (19:29).
crossRefs: Ruth 4:1-10: Boaz acts as kinsman-redeemer at the town gate before ten elders and buys back the land.
Leviticus 25:47-49: A man sold to a foreigner may be bought back by his brother, uncle, cousin or nearest kin.
Numbers 35:19: The avenger of blood, the same word go'el, is the relative charged with the killer's life.
Isaiah 44:6: Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the LORD of Hosts.
Jeremiah 17:1: The sin of Judah is engraved with an iron stylus and a diamond point on the tablet of their hearts.

translationNotes.note: A go'el is a specific job in family law, held by the nearest adult male relative. He buys back land the family had to sell (Leviticus 25:25), buys back a relative sold into servitude (Leviticus 25:47-49), marries a childless widow to raise up the dead man's name (Ruth 4:5-10), and pursues the killer of a murdered kinsman (Numbers 35:19). Every one of those duties is about a man who cannot act for himself. Job has just spent eighteen verses saying his brothers, kinsmen, friends, wife and servants have all abandoned him: there is no go'el left, and that is why he says God is one.

The verb is the courtroom word for a witness or advocate rising to his feet to speak, the same standing up as in Psalm 12:5 and Isaiah 3:13. Combined with go'el in the same sentence, the picture is a legal one: the kinsman rises last, when everyone else has spoken, and states the case for the man who cannot.

translationNotes.term: By the skin of my teeth
translationNotes.note: This verse is the origin of the English phrase, taken from the 1560 Geneva Bible and kept by the King James translators. Teeth have no skin, which is the point: Job says what he escaped with amounts to nothing at all. English speakers now use it to mean a narrow escape, which softens a line that originally meant the margin was zero.

translationNotes.term: Inscribed in a book, on lead, in stone
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר (sefer) - עֵט בַּרְזֶל (et barzel) - עֹפֶרֶת ('oferet)
translationNotes.note: Three writing methods in ascending order of permanence. A sefer is a scroll of leather or papyrus, which rots. An iron stylus cuts letters into soft material. Stone cut and filled with molten lead lasts indefinitely, and monumental inscriptions were made exactly that way. Job is asking for the most durable record technology available to him, because he expects to be dead before the case is heard.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job accuses his friends of tormenting him with words and describes God as his true antagonist, stripping him of honor and isolating him from family and servants. He appeals for pity, wishes his words were recorded forever, declares that his redeemer lives and he will see God, and warns his friends they will face judgment if they continue pursuing him.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 20
summaryBullets: Then Zophar the Naamathite replied: (20:1).
“So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer, because of the turmoil within me. (20:2).
I have heard a rebuke that insults me, and my understanding prompts a reply. (20:3).
Do you not know that from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth, (20:4).
the triumph of the wicked has been brief and the joy of the godless momentary? (20:5).
Though his arrogance reaches the heavens, and his head touches the clouds, (20:6).
he will perish forever, like his own dung; those who had seen him will ask, ‘Where is he?’ (20:7).
He will fly away like a dream, never to be found; he will be chased away like a vision in the night. (20:8).
The eye that saw him will see him no more, and his place will no longer behold him. (20:9).
His sons will seek the favor of the poor, for his own hands must return his wealth. (20:10).
The youthful vigor that fills his bones will lie down with him in the dust. (20:11).
Though evil is sweet in his mouth and he conceals it under his tongue, (20:12).
though he cannot bear to let it go and keeps it in his mouth, (20:13).
yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of cobras within him. (20:14).
He swallows wealth but vomits it out; God will force it from his stomach. (20:15).
He will suck the poison of cobras; the fangs of a viper will kill him. (20:16).
He will not enjoy the streams, the rivers flowing with honey and cream. (20:17).
He must return the fruit of his labor without consuming it; he cannot enjoy the profits of his trading. (20:18).
For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor; he has seized houses he did not build. (20:19).
Because his appetite is never satisfied, he cannot escape with his treasure. (20:20).
Nothing is left for him to consume; thus his prosperity will not endure. (20:21).
In the midst of his plenty, he will be distressed; the full force of misery will come upon him. (20:22).
When he has filled his stomach, God will vent His fury upon him, raining it down on him as he eats. (20:23).
Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him. (20:24).
It is drawn out of his back, the gleaming point from his liver. Terrors come over him. (20:25).
Total darkness is reserved for his treasures. A fire unfanned will consume him and devour what is left in his tent. (20:26).
The heavens will expose his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him. (20:27).
The possessions of his house will be removed, flowing away on the day of God’s wrath. (20:28).
This is the wicked man’s portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him.” (20:29).
crossRefs: Psalm 37:35-36: I saw a ruthless man flourishing like a green tree, and then he was gone and could not be found.
Proverbs 23:31-32: In the end wine bites like a serpent and poisons like a viper.
Habakkuk 2:6-8: Woe to him who piles up what is not his; his creditors will suddenly rise and shake him.
Luke 12:16-21: A rich man plans bigger barns and is told that his life is required of him that night.
Job 21:29-33: Job answers that the wicked man is spared on the day of calamity and buried with a guard on his tomb.

translationNotes.note: Dried animal dung was fuel and it was everywhere, gathered, dried in cakes and burned because firewood was scarce (Ezekiel 4:12-15). Zophar picks the one substance that is universally handled, universally worthless and gone without trace once it burns. The insult is calculated and the audience would have felt it as coarse.

The peten is the Egyptian cobra, which lives across North Africa and the Levant and is the snake shown rearing on Egyptian royal headdresses. Its venom kills by paralysis. Zophar's picture is of swallowed wealth turning to cobra venom in the stomach, then the man sucking on it as if nursing. Isaiah and the Psalms use the same snake (Psalm 58:4; Isaiah 11:8).

The Hebrew says a bow of bronze, meaning a composite bow with horn and sinew laminated to wood, which shot far harder than a plain self bow and could drive a point through armour. Bronze arrowheads survive in the thousands from Late Bronze and Iron Age sites. Verse 24 describes fleeing one weapon straight into the range of a better one.

Every fire in that world had to be started and kept alive by human breath or bellows, so a fire nobody blew on was a fire nobody lit. Zophar means a destruction with no human cause behind it. The same idiom lies behind Daniel's stone cut out without hands (Daniel 2:34).

stories.keyTakeaway: Zophar responds to Job by insisting that the wicked always suffer ruin - their joy is fleeting, their wealth turns to poison, and God brings them down through violence and natural disaster. He argues this is the eternal fate appointed by God for the godless.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 21
summaryBullets: Then Job answered: (21:1).
“Listen carefully to my words; let this be your consolation to me. (21:2).
Bear with me while I speak; then, after I have spoken, you may go on mocking. (21:3).
Is my complaint against a man? Then why should I not be impatient? (21:4).
Look at me and be appalled; put your hand over your mouth. (21:5).
When I remember, terror takes hold, and my body trembles in horror. (21:6).
Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power? (21:7).
Their descendants are established around them, and their offspring before their eyes. (21:8).
Their homes are safe from fear; no rod of punishment from God is upon them. (21:9).
Their bulls breed without fail; their cows bear calves and do not miscarry. (21:10).
They send forth their little ones like a flock; their children skip about, (21:11).
singing to the tambourine and lyre and making merry at the sound of the flute. (21:12).
They spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace. (21:13).
Yet they say to God: ‘Leave us alone! For we have no desire to know Your ways. (21:14).
Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him, and what would we gain if we pray to Him?’ (21:15).
Still, their prosperity is not in their own hands, so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked. (21:16).
How often is the lamp of the wicked put out? Does disaster come upon them? Does God, in His anger, apportion destruction? (21:17).
Are they like straw before the wind, like chaff swept away by a storm? (21:18).
It is said that God lays up one’s punishment for his children. Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it. (21:19).
Let his eyes see his own destruction; let him drink for himself the wrath of the Almighty. (21:20).
For what does he care about his household after him, when the number of his months has run out? (21:21).
Can anyone teach knowledge to God, since He judges those on high? (21:22).
One man dies full of vigor, completely secure and at ease. (21:23).
His body is well nourished, and his bones are rich with marrow. (21:24).
Yet another man dies in the bitterness of his soul, having never tasted prosperity. (21:25).
But together they lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both. (21:26).
Behold, I know your thoughts full well, the schemes by which you would wrong me. (21:27).
For you say, ‘Where now is the nobleman’s house, and where are the tents in which the wicked dwell?’ (21:28).
Have you never asked those who travel the roads? Do you not accept their reports? (21:29).
Indeed, the evil man is spared from the day of calamity, delivered from the day of wrath. (21:30).
Who denounces his behavior to his face? Who repays him for what he has done? (21:31).
He is carried to the grave, and watch is kept over his tomb. (21:32).
The clods of the valley are sweet to him; everyone follows behind him, and those before him are without number. (21:33).
So how can you comfort me with empty words? For your answers remain full of falsehood.” (21:34).
crossRefs: Psalm 73:1-14: Asaph envies the arrogant, who have no struggles, whose bodies are healthy and strong.
Jeremiah 12:1-2: Why does the way of the wicked prosper, and why do all the treacherous thrive?
Malachi 3:14-15: Now we call the arrogant blessed, for evildoers prosper and even test God and escape.
Ecclesiastes 8:14: The righteous get what the wicked deserve, and the wicked what the righteous deserve.
Job 20:4-11: Zophar's flat claim, immediately before this, that the triumph of the wicked is always short.

translationNotes.term: Put your hand over your mouth
translationNotes.note: The recognised gesture of being silenced by something too great to answer. Princes do it before Job in his prime (29:9), and Job himself does it at the end when God has finished speaking (40:4). Micah 7:16 uses it for nations struck dumb. Job is demanding the same posture from his friends that he will finally take before God.

The three instruments of ordinary celebration. The tof is a hand frame drum, usually played by women (Exodus 15:20). The kinnor is a small hand-held lyre with strings across a wooden frame, the instrument David played for Saul. The ugav is a pipe. The same trio marks a household at ease, and Genesis 4:21 names the kinnor and the ugav as the first instruments made.

Two by-products of threshing, and they are not the same thing. Teven is chopped straw, which was kept and fed to animals or mixed into mud brick (Exodus 5:7). Mots is chaff, the light husk that the winnowing fork throws into the evening breeze and that blows away entirely. Job's question in verse 18 is whether the wicked really end up as the worthless one, and his answer is that they do not.

translationNotes.term: Watch is kept over his tomb
translationNotes.note: The rich were buried in rock-cut chamber tombs with the family's bones gathered inside, and the tomb was a permanent monument that could be guarded and visited. Grave robbery was common enough that keeping watch was a real service, not a metaphor. Job's closing insult is that the wicked man not only dies comfortable, he gets a funeral procession and a guarded grave.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job challenges his friends to observe that the wicked often prosper with children, security, and wealth, living long lives in peace while the righteous suffer, and he dismisses their arguments as empty nonsense. He questions why God allows the wicked to die peacefully while others perish in bitterness, and notes that people traveling can confirm the wicked escape calamity and are honored at their deaths.

headings.text: Job: God Will Punish the Wicked

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 22
summaryBullets: Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied: (22:1).
“Can a man be of use to God? Can even a wise man benefit Him? (22:2).
Does it delight the Almighty that you are righteous? Does He profit if your ways are blameless? (22:3).
Is it for your reverence that He rebukes you and enters into judgment against you? (22:4).
Is not your wickedness great? Are not your iniquities endless? (22:5).
For you needlessly demanded security from your brothers and deprived the naked of their clothing. (22:6).
You gave no water to the weary and withheld food from the famished, (22:7).
while the land belonged to a mighty man, and a man of honor lived on it. (22:8).
You sent widows away empty-handed, and the strength of the fatherless was crushed. (22:9).
Therefore snares surround you, and sudden peril terrifies you; (22:10).
it is so dark you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you. (22:11).
Is not God as high as the heavens? Look at the highest stars, how lofty they are! (22:12).
Yet you say: ‘What does God know? Does He judge through thick darkness? (22:13).
Thick clouds veil Him so He does not see us as He traverses the vault of heaven.’ (22:14).
Will you stay on the ancient path that wicked men have trod? (22:15).
They were snatched away before their time, and their foundations were swept away by a flood. (22:16).
They said to God, ‘Depart from us. What can the Almighty do to us?’ (22:17).
But it was He who filled their houses with good things; so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked. (22:18).
The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent mock them: (22:19).
‘Surely our foes are destroyed, and fire has consumed their excess.’ (22:20).
Reconcile now and be at peace with Him; thereby good will come to you. (22:21).
Receive instruction from His mouth, and lay up His words in your heart. (22:22).
If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored. If you remove injustice from your tents (22:23).
and consign your gold to the dust and the gold of Ophir to the stones of the ravines, (22:24).
then the Almighty will be your gold and the finest silver for you. (22:25).
Surely then you will delight in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. (22:26).
You will pray to Him, and He will hear you, and you will fulfill your vows. (22:27).
Your decisions will be carried out, and light will shine on your ways. (22:28).
When men are brought low and you say, ‘Lift them up!’ then He will save the lowly. (22:29).
He will deliver even one who is not innocent, rescuing him through the cleanness of your hands.” (22:30).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 24:10-17: The law on pledges, on paying a hired man the same day, and on the widow's garment.
Exodus 22:26-27: A neighbour's cloak taken in pledge must be returned by sunset, because he sleeps in it.
1 Kings 9:28: Solomon's fleet sails to Ophir and brings back 420 talents of gold.
Ezekiel 18:7-9: The righteous man defined by these exact acts, returning the pledge and feeding the hungry.
Job 31:16-22: Job's oath under curse denying, item by item, every charge Eliphaz makes here.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָבַל (chaval), to take in pledge
translationNotes.note: A poor man borrowing had nothing to pledge but his outer cloak, which was also his blanket. The law therefore ordered the lender to return it every evening (Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:12-13), and a seventh-century BC ostracon found at Yavneh-Yam preserves a labourer's written complaint that his cloak was taken and not returned. Eliphaz is accusing Job of the exact practice the law names, and Job answers it directly at 31:19-20.

Ophir was the source of the finest gold known to Israel, reached by ship from Ezion-geber on the Gulf of Aqaba on voyages that took three years round trip (1 Kings 9:26-28; 10:22). Its location is not established; the sailing route points to Arabia, East Africa or India. That it was a real trading name and not a figure of speech is confirmed by a pottery sherd found at Tell Qasile near modern Tel Aviv, inscribed gold of Ophir for Beth-horon, thirty shekels.

translationNotes.term: Consign your gold to the dust
translationNotes.note: Eliphaz tells Job to throw his gold back into the wadi gravel it was panned out of. Alluvial gold was recovered by washing stream beds, so this is a specific instruction to undo the mining. Verse 25 supplies the exchange: give up the metal and the Almighty becomes your ore. Job takes up real mining at length in chapter 28.

Chug means a circle, the arc a compass draws, and it is the same word in Isaiah 40:22 for the circle of the earth and in Proverbs 8:27 for the circle inscribed on the face of the deep. Eliphaz is quoting what he says the wicked believe: that God walks around the rim of the sky, too far off and too screened by cloud to see what happens below.

stories.keyTakeaway: Eliphaz accuses Job of wickedness - withholding water and food from the needy, stripping people naked, and sending widows away empty - and claims God's darkness hides him from judging such crimes. He urges Job to submit to God, remove wickedness, surrender his wealth, and promises that obedience will restore him to prosperity and answered prayers.

headings.text: Eliphaz: Can a Man Be of Use to God?

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 23
summaryBullets: Then Job answered: (23:1).
“Even today my complaint is bitter. His hand is heavy despite my groaning. (23:2).
If only I knew where to find Him, so that I could go to His seat. (23:3).
I would plead my case before Him and fill my mouth with arguments. (23:4).
I would learn how He would answer, and consider what He would say. (23:5).
Would He contend with me in His great power? No, He would certainly take note of me. (23:6).
Then an upright man could reason with Him, and I would be delivered forever from my Judge. (23:7).
If I go east, He is not there, and if I go west, I cannot find Him. (23:8).
When He is at work in the north, I cannot behold Him; when He turns to the south, I cannot see Him. (23:9).
Yet He knows the way I have taken; when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold. (23:10).
My feet have followed in His tracks; I have kept His way without turning aside. (23:11).
I have not departed from the command of His lips; I have treasured the words of His mouth more than my daily bread. (23:12).
But He is unchangeable, and who can oppose Him? He does what He desires. (23:13).
For He carries out His decree against me, and He has many such plans. (23:14).
Therefore I am terrified in His presence; when I consider this, I fear Him. (23:15).
God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me. (23:16).
Yet I am not silenced by the darkness, by the thick darkness that covers my face. (23:17).
crossRefs: Isaiah 55:6: Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near.
Zechariah 13:9: I will refine them as silver is refined and test them as gold is tested.
Malachi 3:2-3: He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and purify the sons of Levi.
1 Peter 1:6-7: Faith tested by fire, more precious than gold which perishes though refined by fire.
Psalm 139:7-12: Where can I go from Your Spirit; the four directions and the dark are all searched and none hides.

translationNotes.note: The word means a fixed, established place, and the picture is a judge's seat, the bench where a case is actually heard. Job is not looking for a mood or a mountain. He wants the address of the court, and his complaint in verses 3 to 9 is that the court has no findable location, which in ordinary law would end the case before it began.

Hebrew orients by facing east, so the words are literally in front, behind, to the left and to the right. East is forward, west is backward, north is the left hand and south is the right hand. Yemen, the country name, is the same word as right hand, meaning the land to the south. Job is not wandering; he is turning on the spot through all four quarters.

translationNotes.term: I will come forth as gold
translationNotes.note: Bachan is the technical word for testing metal for purity, done by melting ore in a crucible and skimming off the dross. Gold and silver were assayed exactly this way and the vocabulary passed straight into Hebrew for testing people (Psalm 66:10; Proverbs 17:3; Zechariah 13:9). Job is claiming he will survive the fire with nothing burned off, which is a claim about content, not endurance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵחֻקִּי (me-chuqqi), more than my portion
translationNotes.note: Chok here means an allotted ration, the fixed measure of grain issued to a worker or a household. Joseph's priests receive such an allowance from Pharaoh (Genesis 47:22), and Proverbs 30:8 asks for exactly that: feed me with my allotted bread. Job says he has valued God's words above the day's food ration, which in a subsistence economy is the strongest comparison available.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job says he cannot find God anywhere despite searching, yet God knows every step Job takes and will test him like gold; though Job has followed God's commands and kept his words, he remains terrified of God's power and the decrees God carries out against him.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 24
summaryBullets: “Why does the Almighty not reserve times for judgment? Why may those who know Him never see His days? (24:1).
Men move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks. (24:2).
They drive away the donkey of the fatherless and take the widow’s ox in pledge. (24:3).
They push the needy off the road and force all the poor of the land into hiding. (24:4).
Indeed, like wild donkeys in the desert, the poor go to work foraging for food; the wasteland is food for their children. (24:5).
They gather fodder in the fields and glean the vineyards of the wicked. (24:6).
Without clothing, they spend the night naked; they have no covering against the cold. (24:7).
Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rocks for want of shelter. (24:8).
The fatherless infant is snatched from the breast; the nursing child of the poor is seized for a debt. (24:9).
Without clothing, they wander about naked. They carry the sheaves, but still go hungry. (24:10).
They crush olives within their walls; they tread the winepresses, but go thirsty. (24:11).
From the city, men groan, and the souls of the wounded cry out, yet God charges no one with wrongdoing. (24:12).
Then there are those who rebel against the light, not knowing its ways or staying on its paths. (24:13).
When daylight is gone, the murderer rises to kill the poor and needy; in the night he is like a thief. (24:14).
The eye of the adulterer watches for twilight. Thinking, ‘No eye will see me,’ he covers his face. (24:15).
In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves in, never to experience the light. (24:16).
For to them, deep darkness is their morning; surely they are friends with the terrors of darkness! (24:17).
They are but foam on the surface of the water; their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards. (24:18).
As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned. (24:19).
The womb forgets them; the worm feeds on them; they are remembered no more. So injustice is broken like a tree. (24:20).
They prey on the barren and childless, and show no kindness to the widow. (24:21).
Yet by His power, God drags away the mighty; though rising up, they have no assurance of life. (24:22).
He gives them a sense of security, but His eyes are on their ways. (24:23).
They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like heads of grain. (24:24).
If this is not so, then who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?” (24:25).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 19:14: Do not move your neighbour's boundary marker, set up by those who came before you.
Proverbs 22:28: Do not move the ancient boundary stone that your fathers set up.
Deuteronomy 24:19-21: The forgotten sheaf, the olive branch and the fallen grapes are left for the poor and the widow.
Malachi 3:5: I will be a swift witness against those who defraud labourers of their wages and oppress the widow.
Amos 8:4-6: Those who trample the needy, cheat with the ephah and the shekel, and sell the sweepings of the wheat.

translationNotes.note: Fields had no fences. The line between one man's land and the next was marked by stones, and moving them by a pace at a time quietly stole a crop and could not easily be proved. The law names it three times and puts a public curse on it (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17; Proverbs 22:28). In Babylonia the same crime was blocked with carved boundary stones that recorded the grant and called down curses on anyone who shifted them.

Seizing a widow's ox or the donkey of an orphan as loan security took away the animal they ploughed and carried with, so the security destroyed the ability to repay. The law forbids taking a millstone in pledge for the same reason: it would be taking a man's livelihood as security (Deuteronomy 24:6). Job is listing lending practices that were legal in form and ruinous in fact.

translationNotes.term: Glean the vineyards of the wicked
translationNotes.note: Gleaning was a legal right, not charity: the harvester was forbidden to reap the field's corners, go back for a forgotten sheaf, or strip a vine or olive tree twice, and what was left belonged to the poor, the widow, the orphan and the foreigner (Leviticus 19:9-10; Deuteronomy 24:19-21). Ruth lives on it (Ruth 2). Job's protest in verses 6 to 11 is that the poor now glean for the men who are robbing them.

translationNotes.term: Tread the winepresses but go thirsty
translationNotes.note: A winepress was two rock-cut basins, an upper treading floor where grapes were crushed underfoot and a lower vat the juice ran into through a channel. Hundreds are still cut into the bedrock across the hill country. Treading was hot, communal work done at harvest and traditionally accompanied by singing, and the treaders drank. Job's line describes men doing that work and not being allowed a mouthful.

House walls were mud brick, so a thief did not pick a lock, he cut a hole through the wall. The law recognises the crime by that name and rules on a householder who kills a burglar found breaking in at night (Exodus 22:2-3). Jesus uses the same picture of the thief digging through (Matthew 6:19-20; 24:43). Verse 16 is a technical description of a real method.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job catalogs the injustices perpetrated by the wicked - stealing, exploiting the poor and vulnerable, committing murder and adultery under cover of darkness - and argues that despite their temporary success, God ultimately brings them down to death and obscurity.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 25
summaryBullets: Then Bildad the Shuhite replied: (25:1).
“Dominion and awe belong to God; He establishes harmony in the heights of heaven. (25:2).
Can His troops be numbered? On whom does His light not rise? (25:3).
How then can a man be just before God? How can one born of woman be pure? (25:4).
If even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not pure in His sight, (25:5).
how much less man, who is but a maggot, and the son of man, who is but a worm!” (25:6).
crossRefs: Job 4:17-19: Eliphaz's earlier version of this same question about whether a mortal can be pure before God.
Job 15:14-16: Eliphaz repeating it, that even the heavens are not clean in His eyes.
Psalm 8:3-4: When I consider Your heavens, what is man that You are mindful of him?
Isaiah 40:26: Lift up your eyes and see who created these, who brings out the starry host by number and by name.
Psalm 22:6: I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people.

translationNotes.note: The word means raiding parties or armed bands, and applied to heaven it means the host, the assembled armies of God, which is also the sense of LORD of Hosts. Micaiah sees them standing around the throne (1 Kings 22:19), and Daniel counts them as thousands of thousands (Daniel 7:10). Bildad's question is not rhetorical decoration; he is asking whether Job proposes to count them.

Two different creatures. Rimmah is the maggot that breeds in a corpse or in spoiled manna (Exodus 16:20). Tole'ah is the crimson grub, Kermes vermilio, crushed to make the scarlet dye used for the tabernacle curtains and priestly cloth; the same word does duty for the worm and for the colour. Psalm 22:6 uses tole'ah of a person. Bildad picks the two lowest creatures anyone handled.

translationNotes.term: The shortest speech in the book
translationNotes.note: Bildad's third speech runs six verses, against thirty-five and twenty-two in his first two, and Zophar never gets a third speech at all. The friends' arguments physically shrink and then stop, and after this Job speaks without interruption from chapter 26 to chapter 31. The length is part of the record.

The word is shalom, which is far wider than peace as an absence of fighting. It means wholeness, a thing being intact and in working order, and it is used of health, of a settled account and of a treaty. Bildad says God makes shalom in his high places: not quiet, but order that holds.

stories.keyTakeaway: Bildad asserts that God holds dominion and establishes order in the heavens, then argues that no mortal can be righteous or pure before God since even the moon and stars lack brightness in his sight.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 26
summaryBullets: Then Job answered: (26:1).
“How you have helped the powerless and saved the arm that is feeble! (26:2).
How you have counseled the unwise and provided fully sound insight! (26:3).
To whom have you uttered these words? And whose spirit spoke through you? (26:4).
The dead tremble — those beneath the waters and those who dwell in them. (26:5).
Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering. (26:6).
He stretches out the north over empty space; He hangs the earth upon nothing. (26:7).
He wraps up the waters in His clouds, yet the clouds do not burst under their own weight. (26:8).
He covers the face of the full moon, spreading over it His cloud. (26:9).
He has inscribed a horizon on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness. (26:10).
The foundations of heaven quake, astounded at His rebuke. (26:11).
By His power He stirred the sea; by His understanding He shattered Rahab. (26:12).
By His breath the skies were cleared; His hand pierced the fleeing serpent. (26:13).
Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways; how faint is the whisper we hear of Him! Who then can understand the thunder of His power?” (26:14).
crossRefs: Isaiah 40:22: He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth and stretches out the heavens like a canopy.
Proverbs 15:11: Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of men.
Isaiah 51:9: Was it not You who cut Rahab to pieces and pierced the dragon through?
Psalm 89:9-10: You rule the raging sea and still its swelling waves; You crushed Rahab like one of the slain.
Genesis 1:9-10: God gathers the waters into one place and calls the dry ground land.

translationNotes.note: The word means destruction or ruin, used as a name for the realm of the dead in parallel with Sheol. It appears six times in the Old Testament, four of them in Job (26:6; 28:22; 31:12), and Proverbs pairs it with Sheol twice (15:11; 27:20). Revelation 9:11 keeps the Hebrew name and gives its Greek equivalent, Apollyon, the Destroyer.

The surrounding cultures pictured the earth resting on something, on water, on pillars, on the back of a beast. Job's line says it hangs on nothing at all, and the Hebrew coins a word for it: beli-mah, not-anything. It is one of the plainest statements in ancient literature about what holds the world up, and it says the answer is no thing.

translationNotes.term: Inscribed a horizon on the waters
translationNotes.note: The verbs are a draughtsman's: to cut a fixed limit and to scribe a circle. The same picture is at Proverbs 8:27, marking a circle on the face of the deep. From any shore the water ends in a drawn arc, and Job describes that arc as an engraved boundary set where light and darkness divide.

The word means the outer edges or the tips, the hem of a thing rather than the thing. Job ends this survey of creation by calling the whole of it the outermost edge of what God does, and the second half of the verse calls what we hear of Him a whisper. He is measuring everything he has just listed against what has not been shown.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job sarcastically attacks his friends' counsel as worthless, then launches into a description of God's cosmic power over the dead, the waters, the sky, and the sea monsters. He concludes that what they know of God's works is merely the faintest edge of his true magnitude.

headings.text: Job: Who Can Understand God’s Majesty?

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 27
summaryBullets: Job continued his discourse: (27:1).
“As surely as God lives, who has deprived me of justice — the Almighty, who has embittered my soul — (27:2).
as long as my breath is still within me and the breath of God remains in my nostrils, (27:3).
my lips will not speak wickedness, and my tongue will not utter deceit. (27:4).
I will never say that you are right; I will maintain my integrity until I die. (27:5).
I will cling to my righteousness and never let go. As long as I live, my conscience will not accuse me. (27:6).
May my enemy be like the wicked and my opponent like the unjust. (27:7).
For what is the hope of the godless when he is cut off, when God takes away his life? (27:8).
Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him? (27:9).
Will he delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times? (27:10).
I will instruct you in the power of God. I will not conceal the ways of the Almighty. (27:11).
Surely all of you have seen it for yourselves. Why then do you keep up this empty talk? (27:12).
This is the wicked man’s portion from God — the heritage the ruthless receive from the Almighty. (27:13).
Though his sons are many, they are destined for the sword; and his offspring will never have enough food. (27:14).
His survivors will be buried by the plague, and their widows will not weep for them. (27:15).
Though he heaps up silver like dust and piles up a wardrobe like clay, (27:16).
what he lays up, the righteous will wear, and his silver will be divided by the innocent. (27:17).
The house he built is like a moth’s cocoon, like a hut set up by a watchman. (27:18).
He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more; when he opens his eyes, all is gone. (27:19).
Terrors overtake him like a flood; a tempest sweeps him away in the night. (27:20).
The east wind carries him away, and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place. (27:21).
It hurls itself against him without mercy as he flees headlong from its power. (27:22).
It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place. (27:23).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 18:15: As the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, the oath formula Job opens with.
Psalm 26:1-3: Vindicate me, LORD, for I have walked in my integrity and trusted without wavering.
Ecclesiastes 2:18-21: A man leaves everything he worked for to someone who did not work for it.
Proverbs 13:22: The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous.
Isaiah 1:8: Zion left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber field, the image at Job 27:18.

translationNotes.note: The standard binding oath formula in Hebrew, staking the speaker's own standing on the truth of what follows. Elijah uses it (1 Kings 18:15), Hannah uses it (1 Samuel 1:26), and the law treats a false oath in God's name as a capital offence against the third commandment. Job opens his last speech by swearing, which turns everything after it into sworn testimony rather than argument.

translationNotes.term: My conscience will not accuse me
translationNotes.note: Hebrew has no word for conscience. The line says his heart will not reproach him for any of his days, and heart in Hebrew means the seat of thought and decision rather than feeling. Job is saying his own judgment, reviewing his record, returns no charge, which is the claim he will put under oath in chapter 31.

A shelter with the structural strength of a moth's case: it lasts one season and it disintegrates. The parallel line names the other example, the watchman's booth, so the two images belong together as things nobody builds to keep.

translationNotes.term: A hut set up by a watchman
translationNotes.note: At harvest a grower slept in his vineyard or melon field to keep off thieves and animals, in a brush shelter of branches thrown up for the weeks of the crop and abandoned after. Isaiah uses the same picture for a stripped Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:8). It is the same word as the booths of the autumn feast (Leviticus 23:42). Job's point is that the wicked man builds his house to the standard of a shed you leave behind.

translationNotes.term: It claps its hands at him
translationNotes.note: Clapping and hissing were the recognised public gestures of derision at someone's downfall, not applause. Passers-by hiss and shake their heads at ruined Jerusalem (Lamentations 2:15-16; Jeremiah 19:8). Job gives both gestures to the east wind, so that the storm itself jeers the man out of his own doorway.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job swears he will maintain his integrity and never admit his friends are right, then describes the fate God assigns to the wicked: their children face the sword, their wealth is stripped away, and they are swept away by terrors like a violent wind.

stories.title: 📜 Job 28
summaryBullets: “Surely there is a mine for silver and a place where gold is refined. (28:1).
Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore. (28:2).
Man puts an end to the darkness; he probes the farthest recesses for ore in deepest darkness. (28:3).
Far from human habitation he cuts a shaft in places forgotten by the foot of man. Far from men he dangles and sways. (28:4).
Food may come from the earth, but from below it is transformed as by fire. (28:5).
Its rocks are the source of sapphires, containing flecks of gold. (28:6).
No bird of prey knows that path; no falcon’s eye has seen it. (28:7).
Proud beasts have never trodden it; no lion has ever prowled over it. (28:8).
The miner strikes the flint; he overturns mountains at their base. (28:9).
He hews out channels in the rocks, and his eyes spot every treasure. (28:10).
He stops up the sources of the streams to bring what is hidden to light. (28:11).
But where can wisdom be found, and where does understanding dwell? (28:12).
No man can know its value, nor is it found in the land of the living. (28:13).
The ocean depths say, ‘It is not in me,’ while the sea declares, ‘It is not with me.’ (28:14).
It cannot be bought with gold, nor can its price be weighed out in silver. (28:15).
It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire. (28:16).
Neither gold nor crystal can compare to it, nor jewels of fine gold be exchanged for it. (28:17).
Coral and quartz are unworthy of mention; the price of wisdom is beyond rubies. (28:18).
Topaz from Cush cannot compare to it, nor can it be valued in pure gold. (28:19).
From where, then, does wisdom come, and where does understanding dwell? (28:20).
It is hidden from the eyes of every living thing and concealed from the birds of the air. (28:21).
Abaddon and Death say, ‘We have heard a rumor about it.’ (28:22).
But God understands its way, and He knows its place. (28:23).
For He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens. (28:24).
When God fixed the weight of the wind and measured out the waters, (28:25).
when He set a limit for the rain and a path for the thunderbolt, (28:26).
then He looked at wisdom and appraised it; He established it and searched it out. (28:27).
And He said to man, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.’” (28:28).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 8:9: A land whose stones are iron and out of whose hills you can dig copper.
Proverbs 3:13-15: Wisdom brings better returns than silver and is more precious than rubies.
Proverbs 9:10: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
1 Kings 10:11: Hiram's fleet brings gold from Ophir along with great cargoes of almugwood and precious stones.
Isaiah 40:12-14: Who measured the waters in the hollow of His hand, and who taught Him the path of understanding?

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּרַץ נַחַל (parats nachal), to break open a shaft
translationNotes.note: This chapter is a technically accurate description of Bronze and Iron Age hard-rock mining. At Timna in the Arabah, north of the Gulf of Aqaba, thousands of copper mine shafts were cut through the rock, some more than thirty metres deep, with footholds carved into the sides and horizontal galleries running off them. Job's phrases match the workings item for item: the shaft sunk far from anywhere, the men hanging on ropes, the galleries driven through rock, the water dammed back.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דַּלּוּ מֵאֱנוֹשׁ נָעוּ (dallu me-enosh na'u)
translationNotes.note: Miners were lowered down the shaft on ropes and worked hanging, swinging clear of the walls, with the daylight and the rest of the human race above them. Verse 4 is the only description of that job anywhere in Scripture, and it is written by someone who had either watched it or been told by someone who had.

Fire-setting was the standard way to break hard rock before explosives: pile brushwood against the face, burn it hot, then quench the rock with water so it cracks and can be levered out. Verse 5 sets the tilled surface, where food grows, against the underside of the same ground being turned over by fire, and verse 9 adds the miner overturning mountains at their roots.

Not the modern sapphire. The stone meant here is lapis lazuli, a deep blue rock flecked with gold-coloured pyrite, which is exactly what verse 6 describes: its rocks are the place of sappir, and it holds dust of gold. Lapis came from one district, Badakhshan in what is now northeast Afghanistan, and was traded across the whole ancient world from there. It is the stone under God's feet at Exodus 24:10.

translationNotes.term: He stops up the sources of the streams
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִבְּכִי נְהָרוֹת חִבֵּשׁ (mi-bekhi neharot chibbesh)
translationNotes.note: Groundwater breaking into a working is the oldest way to lose a mine, so miners dammed and diverted the seeps to keep the face dry. The Hebrew literally says he binds up the weeping of the rivers. Verse 11 finishes the sequence that began with the shaft: dewater the workings and the hidden ore can be brought out into the light.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job describes how humans mine precious metals and gemstones from deep in the earth, then contrasts this with wisdom, which cannot be found or purchased anywhere and is known only to God; fearing the Lord and shunning evil constitute true wisdom.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 29
summaryBullets: And Job continued his discourse: (29:1).
“How I long for the months gone by, for the days when God watched over me, (29:2).
when His lamp shone above my head, and by His light I walked through the darkness, (29:3).
when I was in my prime, when the friendship of God rested on my tent, (29:4).
when the Almighty was still with me and my children were around me, (29:5).
when my steps were bathed in cream and the rock poured out for me streams of oil! (29:6).
When I went out to the city gate and took my seat in the public square, (29:7).
the young men saw me and withdrew, and the old men rose to their feet. (29:8).
The princes refrained from speaking and covered their mouths with their hands. (29:9).
The voices of the nobles were hushed, and their tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths. (29:10).
For those who heard me called me blessed, and those who saw me commended me, (29:11).
because I rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper. (29:12).
The dying man blessed me, and I made the widow’s heart sing for joy. (29:13).
I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban. (29:14).
I served as eyes to the blind and as feet to the lame. (29:15).
I was a father to the needy, and I took up the case of the stranger. (29:16).
I shattered the fangs of the unjust and snatched the prey from his teeth. (29:17).
So I thought: ‘I will die in my nest and multiply my days as the sand. (29:18).
My roots will spread out to the waters, and the dew will rest nightly on my branches. (29:19).
My glory is ever new within me, and my bow is renewed in my hand.’ (29:20).
Men listened to me with expectation, waiting silently for my counsel. (29:21).
After my words, they spoke no more; my speech settled on them like dew. (29:22).
They waited for me as for rain and drank in my words like spring showers. (29:23).
If I smiled at them, they did not believe it; the light of my countenance was precious. (29:24).
I chose their course and presided as chief. So I dwelt as a king among his troops, as a comforter of the mourners. (29:25).
crossRefs: Ruth 4:1-2: Boaz goes up to the gate and seats ten elders of the town to settle the case in public.
Proverbs 31:23: Her husband is known in the gates, where he sits among the elders of the land.
Amos 5:12,15: They oppress the righteous in the gate; establish justice in the gate instead.
Psalm 72:12-14: The king rescues the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no one to help.
Deuteronomy 33:24: Let Asher be favoured and dip his foot in oil, the picture of plenty behind Job 29:6.

translationNotes.note: The gate was the town's courthouse, market and council chamber in one. Excavated gates at Dan, Gezer, Megiddo and Beersheba are long passages with two or three chambers to each side, fitted with stone benches, and there is usually an open plaza just inside. Elders sat there to hear cases, witness sales and settle disputes, and everything was done in the open so that the crowd was the record. Job describing where he sat is describing his legal standing, not his social life.

translationNotes.term: Streams of oil from the rock
translationNotes.note: Olive trees grow in thin soil over limestone, and the presses were cut into the bedrock itself: a basin to crush the fruit under a rolling stone, then a beam or weighted press to squeeze the pulp. Oil literally ran out of rock. It was the region's main export as well as its cooking fat, lamp fuel and medicine, so the phrase means income, not luxury.

translationNotes.term: Justice was my robe and my turban
translationNotes.note: A tsanif is a wound headcloth, the headgear of high office; the same word is used of a royal diadem (Isaiah 62:3) and of the high priest's turban (Zechariah 3:5). Clothing was the visible statement of rank in a world with no other identification. Job says the office he wore in public was righteousness, which is a claim about his conduct on the bench in verse 7.

translationNotes.term: I took up the case of the stranger
translationNotes.note: A stranger, a widow and an orphan share one legal problem: no adult male relative to speak for them, and cases were argued by kinsmen in person. That is why Scripture names those three together again and again (Exodus 22:21-22; Deuteronomy 24:17). Job says he took the file of a man with no family in town, which was unpaid work with nothing in it for him.

A settled proverb for dying at home, old, among your own people, with the household intact around you. Balaam uses the same nest image for a secure people (Numbers 24:21), and Obadiah for Edom's cliff strongholds (Obadiah 1:4). Job's expectation in verse 18 is the ordinary hope of a patriarch, and chapter 30 opens by taking it apart.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job recalls his former prosperity and respect; he was honored in the city gate, helped the poor and afflicted, and his counsel was sought and valued like rain in drought.

stories.title: 🗣️ Job 30
summaryBullets: “But now they mock me, men younger than I am, whose fathers I would have refused to put with my sheep dogs. (30:1).
What use to me was the strength of their hands, since their vigor had left them? (30:2).
Gaunt from poverty and hunger, they gnawed the dry land, and the desolate wasteland by night. (30:3).
They plucked mallow among the shrubs, and the roots of the broom tree were their food. (30:4).
They were banished from among men, shouted at like thieves, (30:5).
so that they lived on the slopes of the wadis, among the rocks and in holes in the ground. (30:6).
They cried out among the shrubs and huddled beneath the nettles. (30:7).
A senseless and nameless brood, they were driven off the land. (30:8).
And now they mock me in song; I have become a byword among them. (30:9).
They abhor me and keep far from me; they do not hesitate to spit in my face. (30:10).
Because God has unstrung my bow and afflicted me, they have cast off restraint in my presence. (30:11).
The rabble arises at my right; they lay snares for my feet and build siege ramps against me. (30:12).
They tear up my path; they profit from my destruction, with no one to restrain them. (30:13).
They advance as through a wide breach; through the ruins they keep rolling in. (30:14).
Terrors are turned loose against me; they drive away my dignity as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed like a cloud. (30:15).
And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction grip me. (30:16).
Night pierces my bones, and my gnawing pains never rest. (30:17).
With great force He grasps my garment; He seizes me by the collar of my tunic. (30:18).
He throws me into the mud, and I have become like dust and ashes. (30:19).
I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer; when I stand up, You merely look at me. (30:20).
You have ruthlessly turned on me; You oppose me with Your strong hand. (30:21).
You snatch me up into the wind and drive me before it; You toss me about in the storm. (30:22).
Yes, I know that You will bring me down to death, to the place appointed for all the living. (30:23).
Yet no one stretches out his hand against a ruined man when he cries for help in his distress. (30:24).
Have I not wept for those in trouble? Has my soul not grieved for the needy? (30:25).
But when I hoped for good, evil came; when I looked for light, darkness fell. (30:26).
I am churning within and cannot rest; days of affliction confront me. (30:27).
I go about blackened, but not by the sun. I stand up in the assembly and cry for help. (30:28).
I have become a brother of jackals, a companion of ostriches. (30:29).
My skin grows black and peels, and my bones burn with fever. (30:30).
My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping. (30:31).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 19:4-5: Elijah sits down under a broom tree in the wilderness and asks to die.
Psalm 102:6-7: I am like a desert owl, like an owl among the ruins, awake and alone on a roof.
Lamentations 5:14-15: The elders have left the gate; our dancing has turned to mourning.
Micah 1:8: I will howl like the jackals and mourn like the ostriches.
Psalm 69:11-12: I made sackcloth my clothing, and I became the talk of the town and the song of the drunkards.

translationNotes.note: The only mention in the Old Testament of dogs working with flocks, and it appears in an insult. Dogs elsewhere in Scripture are scavengers that eat the dead in the street (1 Kings 21:23), and calling a man a dog was a serious contempt (1 Samuel 17:43; 2 Samuel 9:8). Job says these men's fathers were not fit to be put with the animals nobody respected.

Two real desert plants and both are famine food. Malluach is saltbush, a grey shrub of salt flats whose leaves can be eaten and taste of salt. Rotem is the white broom, a leafless shrub of dry wadis whose roots are bitter and barely edible; its wood makes the hottest, longest-burning charcoal of the region, which is why Psalm 120:4 names coals of the broom tree. Elijah sits under one (1 Kings 19:4). Job is describing people eating what nobody eats.

A siege ramp was an earth and rubble embankment built up against a city wall so that a battering ram could be pushed to the top of it. The Assyrian ramp at Lachish, built by Sennacherib in 701 BC, still stands and is shown under construction on the palace reliefs from Nineveh. Job uses this three times of himself (19:12; 30:12), which casts his body as a walled town under professional attack.

translationNotes.term: A brother of jackals, a companion of ostriches
translationNotes.note: Both are named for the noise they make at night in empty country. The jackal's rising howl and the ostrich's low booming call are the sounds of a place with no people, which is why the prophets list these two together as the new residents of a ruined city (Isaiah 34:13; Micah 1:8). Job says he has joined that company: not that he is sad, but that he now belongs where towns used to be.

translationNotes.term: I go about blackened, but not by the sun
translationNotes.note: The word means darkened, and it is the standard term for going about in mourning dress with the head covered and unwashed (Psalm 35:14; Jeremiah 8:21). Job blocks the obvious reading in the same breath: this is not a farmer's tan. Verse 30 supplies the physical cause, skin blackening and peeling off him.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job describes how men younger and more contemptible than himself now mock him in song, attack him without restraint, and keep their distance; he suffers physically as God afflicts him and does not answer his cries, leaving him blackened, fevered, and reduced to mourning.

stories.title: ⚖️ Job 31
summaryBullets: “I have made a covenant with my eyes. How then could I gaze with desire at a virgin? (31:1).
For what is the allotment of God from above, or the heritage from the Almighty on high? (31:2).
Does not disaster come to the unjust and calamity to the workers of iniquity? (31:3).
Does He not see my ways and count my every step? (31:4).
If I have walked in falsehood or my foot has rushed to deceit, (31:5).
let God weigh me with honest scales, that He may know my integrity. (31:6).
If my steps have turned from the path, if my heart has followed my eyes, or if impurity has stuck to my hands, (31:7).
then may another eat what I have sown, and may my crops be uprooted. (31:8).
If my heart has been enticed by my neighbor’s wife, or I have lurked at his door, (31:9).
then may my own wife grind grain for another, and may other men sleep with her. (31:10).
For that would be a heinous crime, an iniquity to be judged. (31:11).
For it is a fire that burns down to Abaddon; it would root out my entire harvest. (31:12).
If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or maidservant when they made a complaint against me, (31:13).
what will I do when God rises to judge? How will I answer when called to account? (31:14).
Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb? (31:15).
If I have denied the desires of the poor or allowed the widow’s eyes to fail, (31:16).
if I have eaten my morsel alone, not sharing it with the fatherless — (31:17).
though from my youth I reared him as would a father, and from my mother’s womb I guided the widow — (31:18).
if I have seen one perish for lack of clothing, or a needy man without a cloak, (31:19).
if his heart has not blessed me for warming him with the fleece of my sheep, (31:20).
if I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless because I saw that I had support in the gate, (31:21).
then may my arm fall from my shoulder and be torn from its socket. (31:22).
For calamity from God terrifies me, and His splendor I cannot overpower. (31:23).
If I have put my trust in gold or called pure gold my security, (31:24).
if I have rejoiced in my great wealth because my hand had gained so much, (31:25).
if I have beheld the sun in its radiance or the moon moving in splendor, (31:26).
so that my heart was secretly enticed and my hand threw a kiss from my mouth, (31:27).
this would also be an iniquity to be judged, for I would have denied God on high. (31:28).
If I have rejoiced in my enemy’s ruin, or exulted when evil befell him — (31:29).
I have not allowed my mouth to sin by asking for his life with a curse — (31:30).
if the men of my house have not said, ‘Who is there who has not had his fill?’— (31:31).
but no stranger had to lodge on the street, for my door has been open to the traveler — (31:32).
if I have covered my transgressions like Adam by hiding my guilt in my heart, (31:33).
because I greatly feared the crowds and the contempt of the clans terrified me, so that I kept silent and would not go outside — (31:34).
(Oh, that I had one to hear me! Here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me; let my accuser compose an indictment. (31:35).
Surely I would carry it on my shoulder and wear it like a crown. (31:36).
I would give account of all my steps; I would approach Him like a prince.)— (31:37).
if my land cries out against me and its furrows weep together, (31:38).
if I have devoured its produce without payment or broken the spirit of its tenants, (31:39).
then let briers grow instead of wheat and stinkweed instead of barley.” Thus conclude the words of Job. (31:40).
crossRefs: Exodus 20:17: You shall not covet your neighbour's wife, or his servant, or anything that is your neighbour's.
Leviticus 19:35-36: Use honest scales, honest weights, an honest ephah and an honest hin.
Deuteronomy 4:19: Do not be enticed into bowing down to the sun, the moon and the stars.
Genesis 3:8-10: Adam hides among the trees of the garden after he eats, the act Job names at 31:33.
Hebrews 13:2: Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, the duty Job claims at 31:32.

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew is literally here is my tav, my mark. Tav is the last letter of the alphabet, and in the older Hebrew script it was written as a cross or an X, which is why it served as the mark a man made in place of a signature. Ezekiel 9:4 uses the same letter as a mark set on foreheads. Job is signing the bottom of a sworn document and pushing it across the table.

translationNotes.term: Let my accuser compose an indictment
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew says the man of my lawsuit, meaning the opposing party, and asks him to write out a sefer, a formal written charge. Verse 36 says Job would carry that charge on his shoulder and wear it as a crown, that is, display it publicly rather than hide it, because he expects the written accusation to be answerable. This chapter is the closing argument of the lawsuit Job filed at 13:18.

Every transaction was weighed, since there was no coinage, so a merchant carried a pouch of stone weights and the temptation was to carry two sets, heavy for buying and light for selling. The law bans it outright (Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16), and Proverbs 11:1 calls a false balance an abomination. Job asks to be weighed on the honest set.

This is the actual gesture of worship to the sun and moon: raise the hand to the mouth and kiss it toward the object. Elijah is told of seven thousand in Israel whose mouths have not kissed Baal (1 Kings 19:18), and Hosea 13:2 describes men kissing calves. The sun and moon were the chief gods of Mesopotamia, Shamash and Sin, with great temples at Sippar, Ur and Harran. Job's oath in verses 26 to 28 denies not admiration of a sunrise but participation in that cult, and he calls it denying God on high.

The Hebrew phrase can be read as like Adam or as in the way people do, since adam is both the name and the word for mankind. Either reading points at the same behaviour, hiding a fault instead of stating it, and the first instance of it is Genesis 3:8-10. Job's oath denies the concealment, which is the whole basis of his demand for an open trial.

stories.keyTakeaway: Job lists a series of covenants he has kept - avoiding lust, maintaining honesty, showing justice to servants, caring for the poor and widow, rejecting idolatry and wealth-worship, refusing to gloat over enemies' misfortune, and being hospitable - then declares his words finished and expresses his desire for God to answer his accusations.

stories.title: 🗯️ Job 32
summaryBullets: So these three men stopped answering Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes. (32:1).
This kindled the anger of Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram. He burned with anger against Job for justifying himself rather than God, (32:2).
and he burned with anger against Job’s three friends because they had failed to refute Job, and yet had condemned him. (32:3).
Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because the others were older than he. (32:4).
But when he saw that the three men had no further reply, his anger was kindled. (32:5).
So Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite declared: “I am young in years, while you are old; that is why I was timid and afraid to tell you what I know. (32:6).
I thought that age should speak, and many years should teach wisdom. (32:7).
But there is a spirit in a man, the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding. (32:8).
It is not only the old who are wise, or the elderly who understand justice. (32:9).
Therefore I say, ‘Listen to me; I too will declare what I know.’ (32:10).
Indeed, I waited while you spoke; I listened to your reasoning; as you searched for words, (32:11).
I paid you full attention. But no one proved Job wrong; not one of you rebutted his arguments. (32:12).
So do not claim, ‘We have found wisdom; let God, not man, refute him.’ (32:13).
But Job has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your arguments. (32:14).
Job’s friends are dismayed, with no more to say; words have escaped them. (32:15).
Must I wait, now that they are silent, now that they stand and no longer reply? (32:16).
I too will answer; yes, I will declare what I know. (32:17).
For I am full of words, and my spirit within me compels me. (32:18).
Behold, my belly is like unvented wine; it is about to burst like a new wineskin. (32:19).
I must speak and find relief; I must open my lips and respond. (32:20).
I will be partial to no one, nor will I flatter any man. (32:21).
For I do not know how to flatter, or my Maker would remove me in an instant. (32:22).
crossRefs: Job 15:10: Eliphaz claims the grey-haired and the aged are on their side, the seniority Elihu now sets aside.
Proverbs 16:31: Grey hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in the way of righteousness.
1 Timothy 4:12: Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example.
Matthew 9:17: New wine is poured into new wineskins, or the skins burst and the wine is lost.
Genesis 22:20-21: Buz born to Nahor, brother of Uz, the line Elihu the Buzite is named from.

translationNotes.note: Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and brother of Uz (Genesis 22:20-21), which puts Elihu's people in the same family and the same country as Job's. Jeremiah lists Buz beside Dedan and Tema among the desert peoples who shave their temples (Jeremiah 25:23), all of them north Arabian. Every one of the five men in this book is placed by name in that same arc of country east and south of Canaan.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָמִים יְדַבֵּרוּ (yamim yedabberu), let days speak
translationNotes.note: Seniority in years carried formal authority to speak first, and Elihu observes it for thirty-one chapters before opening his mouth. The law puts it in a command: rise before the grey head and honour the face of an old man (Leviticus 19:32). Elihu's whole preface is an apology for breaking a rule of order that his hearers took seriously.

New wine was stored in whole animal skins, sewn shut and pitched. It kept fermenting, gas built up, and a skin that had already been stretched once had no give left and burst. This is exactly the picture Jesus uses of new wine in old skins (Matthew 9:17). Elihu says his belly is a sealed skin at the point of splitting, which is a physical image everyone had cleaned up after.

translationNotes.term: I do not know how to flatter
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲכַנֶּה (akhanneh), to give an honorific title
translationNotes.note: The verb means to bestow a flattering title on someone, the way a courtier addresses a patron. Isaiah 44:5 and 45:4 use it for God giving a name of honour. Elihu is not claiming to be blunt by temperament; he is saying he does not know how to hand out the honorary forms of address that keep a man on the right side of the powerful.

stories.keyTakeaway: Elihu, a younger man who had stayed silent until now, becomes angry at Job for justifying himself over God and at the three friends for failing to refute Job; he declares himself ready to speak and insists he will do so impartially, driven by an inner compulsion to make his case.

stories.title: 🗯️ Job 33
summaryBullets: “But now, O Job, hear my speech, and listen to all my words. (33:1).
Behold, I will open my mouth; my address is on the tip of my tongue. (33:2).
My words are from an upright heart, and my lips speak sincerely what I know. (33:3).
The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life. (33:4).
Refute me if you can; prepare your case and confront me. (33:5).
I am just like you before God; I was also formed from clay. (33:6).
Surely no fear of me should terrify you; nor will my hand be heavy upon you. (33:7).
Surely you have spoken in my hearing, and I have heard these very words: (33:8).
‘I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, with no iniquity in me. (33:9).
Yet God finds occasions against me; He counts me as His enemy. (33:10).
He puts my feet in the stocks; He watches over all my paths.’ (33:11).
Behold, you are not right in this matter. I will answer you, for God is greater than man. (33:12).
Why do you complain to Him that He answers nothing a man asks? (33:13).
For God speaks in one way and in another, yet no one notices. (33:14).
In a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men as they slumber on their beds, (33:15).
He opens their ears and terrifies them with warnings (33:16).
to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride, (33:17).
to preserve his soul from the Pit and his life from perishing by the sword. (33:18).
A man is also chastened on his bed with pain and constant distress in his bones, (33:19).
so that he detests his bread, and his soul loathes his favorite food. (33:20).
His flesh wastes away from sight, and his hidden bones protrude. (33:21).
He draws near to the Pit, and his life to the messengers of death. (33:22).
Yet if there is a messenger on his side, one mediator in a thousand, to tell a man what is right for him, (33:23).
to be gracious to him and say, ‘Spare him from going down to the Pit; I have found his ransom,’ (33:24).
then his flesh is refreshed like a child’s; he returns to the days of his youth. (33:25).
He prays to God and finds favor; he sees God’s face and shouts for joy, and God restores His righteousness to that man. (33:26).
Then he sings before men with these words: ‘I have sinned and perverted what was right; yet I did not get what I deserved. (33:27).
He redeemed my soul from going down to the Pit, and I will live to see the light.’ (33:28).
Behold, all these things God does to a man, two or even three times, (33:29).
to bring back his soul from the Pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of life. (33:30).
Pay attention, Job, and listen to me; be silent, and I will speak. (33:31).
But if you have something to say, answer me; speak up, for I would like to vindicate you. (33:32).
But if not, then listen to me; be quiet, and I will teach you wisdom.” (33:33).
crossRefs: Genesis 20:3: God comes to Abimelech in a dream by night and warns him that he is a dead man.
Numbers 12:6: If there is a prophet among you, I make Myself known to him in a vision and speak in a dream.
Exodus 21:30: If a ransom is imposed on him, he shall pay whatever is demanded for the redemption of his life.
Psalm 49:7-8: No man can redeem another or give God a ransom for him; the price of a life is too costly.
Job 9:33: Job's own wish for an arbiter, which Elihu now answers with the messenger of 33:23.

translationNotes.note: A melits is an interpreter or spokesman, the man who stands between two parties who cannot deal directly. The same word is used of the interpreter between Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 42:23) and of the envoys sent to Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 32:31). Elihu is answering Job's demand at 9:33 for an arbitrator, and he answers with an office rather than a person.

A kofer is a payment made in place of a life that is legally forfeit. If a known goring ox kills a man, the owner is under sentence and a kofer may be set instead (Exodus 21:29-30). Every Israelite counted in the census pays a half shekel as kofer for his life (Exodus 30:12). And no kofer may ever be taken for a murderer (Numbers 35:31). The word means an accepted substitute payment, not a fee or a bribe.

Shachat means a pit and specifically a trap pit dug for large animals and covered over. Used of death, it carries that sense of a hole you fall into and cannot climb out of, and it stands parallel to Sheol throughout the Psalms (Psalm 16:10; 30:9). Elihu repeats it five times in this chapter, which is the drumbeat of his argument.

translationNotes.term: I was also formed from clay
translationNotes.note: The verb qarats means to pinch or nip off, exactly what a potter does when he takes a lump from the mass to throw a vessel. Elihu picks up Job's own image from 10:9 and applies it to himself, to say that Job is not facing God directly in this conversation but a man made the same way. It is an offer to be the safe substitute for the terrifying interview Job asked for.

stories.keyTakeaway: Elihu claims God speaks through dreams and physical suffering to turn people from wrongdoing, and argues that Job is wrong to say God ignores human words or that he himself is pure while God treats him as an enemy. He invites Job to respond or listen while he explains God's wisdom.

stories.title: 🗯️ Job 34
summaryBullets: Then Elihu continued: (34:1).
“Hear my words, O wise men; give ear to me, O men of learning. (34:2).
For the ear tests words as the mouth tastes food. (34:3).
