Let us choose for ourselves what is right; let us learn together what is good. (34:4).
For Job has declared, ‘I am righteous, yet God has deprived me of justice. (34:5).
Would I lie about my case? My wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.’ (34:6).
What man is like Job, who drinks up derision like water? (34:7).
He keeps company with evildoers and walks with wicked men. (34:8).
For he has said, ‘It profits a man nothing that he should delight in God.’ (34:9).
Therefore listen to me, O men of understanding. Far be it from God to do wrong, and from the Almighty to act unjustly. (34:10).
For according to a man’s deeds He repays him; according to a man’s ways He brings consequences. (34:11).
Indeed, it is true that God does not act wickedly, and the Almighty does not pervert justice. (34:12).
Who gave Him charge over the earth? Who appointed Him over the whole world? (34:13).
If He were to set His heart to it and withdraw His Spirit and breath, (34:14).
all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust. (34:15).
If you have understanding, hear this; listen to my words. (34:16).
Could one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn the just and mighty One, (34:17).
who says to kings, ‘You are worthless!’ and to nobles, ‘You are wicked,’ (34:18).
who is not partial to princes and does not favor rich over poor? For they are all the work of His hands. (34:19).
They die in an instant, in the middle of the night. The people convulse and pass away; the mighty are removed without human hand. (34:20).
For His eyes are on the ways of a man, and He sees his every step. (34:21).
There is no darkness or deep shadow where the workers of iniquity can hide. (34:22).
For God need not examine a man further or have him approach for judgment. (34:23).
He shatters the mighty without inquiry and sets up others in their place. (34:24).
Therefore, He recognizes their deeds; He overthrows them in the night and they are crushed. (34:25).
He strikes them for their wickedness in full view, (34:26).
because they turned aside from Him and had no regard for any of His ways. (34:27).
They caused the cry of the poor to come before Him, and He heard the outcry of the afflicted. (34:28).
But when He remains silent, who can condemn Him? When He hides His face, who can see Him? Yet He watches over both man and nation, (34:29).
that godless men should not rule or lay snares for the people. (34:30).
Suppose someone says to God, ‘I have endured my punishment; I will offend no more. (34:31).
Teach me what I cannot see; if I have done wrong, I will not do it again.’ (34:32).
Should God repay you on your own terms when you have disavowed Him? You must choose, not I; so tell me what you know. (34:33).
Men of understanding will declare to me, and the wise men who hear me will say: (34:34).
‘Job speaks without knowledge; his words lack insight.’ (34:35).
If only Job were tried to the utmost for answering like a wicked man. (34:36).
For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God.” (34:37).
crossRefs: Genesis 18:25: Far be it from You; will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?
Deuteronomy 32:4: All His ways are just, a God of faithfulness and without injustice, upright and true.
Proverbs 5:21: A man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and He examines all his paths.
Psalm 33:13-15: The LORD looks down from heaven and considers everything the sons of men do.
Romans 3:5-6: If our unrighteousness brings out God's righteousness, is God unjust? Then how could He judge the world?

translationNotes.term: Hear my words, O wise men
translationNotes.note: Elihu addresses a wider audience than the three friends. Wisdom was a recognised profession across the ancient Near East, with schools, collections of sayings and international reputations; 1 Kings 4:30 measures Solomon against the wisdom of the sons of the east and of Egypt. This whole book is a debate conducted in that professional world, which is why every speaker argues from observation and proverb rather than from law or prophecy.

Both words mean breath, and both do double duty for wind and for the life in a body. Elihu's argument in verses 14 and 15 runs on that: what animates a man is on loan, and if it is drawn back all flesh stops together. Genesis 2:7 uses neshamah for what God breathes into the man, and Genesis 7:22 uses both words together for what dies in the flood.

Beliyaal is one of Hebrew's hardest words, meaning worthlessness or ruin, and it is used of the worst characters in Scripture: the men of Gibeah (Judges 19:22), Eli's sons (1 Samuel 2:12), Nabal (1 Samuel 25:17). Later Greek writers took it over as a name, Belial, which is how Paul uses it at 2 Corinthians 6:15. Elihu says God addresses kings with the word reserved for the lowest men there are.

translationNotes.term: In the middle of the night
translationNotes.note: The night was reckoned in watches, and midnight is the point Scripture repeatedly attaches to sudden divine action: the death of the firstborn (Exodus 12:29), Samson lifting the gates of Gaza (Judges 16:3), the earthquake at Philippi (Acts 16:25-26). Elihu picks the hour at which no one is on guard and no court is sitting.

stories.keyTakeaway: Elihu argues that God cannot do wrong and repays everyone according to their conduct; he accuses Job of speaking without knowledge and of adding rebellion to his sin by complaining against God.

stories.title: 🗯️ Job 35
summaryBullets: And Elihu went on to say: (35:1).
“Do you think this is just? You say, ‘I am more righteous than God.’ (35:2).
For you ask, ‘What does it profit me, and what benefit do I gain apart from sin?’ (35:3).
I will reply to you and to your friends as well. (35:4).
Look to the heavens and see; gaze at the clouds high above you. (35:5).
If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him? If you multiply your transgressions, what do you do to Him? (35:6).
If you are righteous, what do you give Him, or what does He receive from your hand? (35:7).
Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a son of man. (35:8).
Men cry out under great oppression; they plead for relief from the arm of the mighty. (35:9).
But no one asks, ‘Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night, (35:10).
who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the air?’ (35:11).
There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men. (35:12).
Surely God does not listen to empty pleas, and the Almighty does not take note of it. (35:13).
How much less, then, when you say that you do not see Him, that your case is before Him and you must wait for Him, (35:14).
and further, that in His anger He has not punished or taken much notice of folly! (35:15).
So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge.” (35:16).
crossRefs: Psalm 42:8: At night His song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.
Proverbs 9:12: If you are wise, your wisdom rewards you; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.
Isaiah 1:15: When you spread out your hands I will hide My eyes from you; your hands are full of blood.
Psalm 66:18: If I had cherished sin in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.
Job 22:2-3: Eliphaz asked the same question first, whether a man's righteousness is of any profit to God.

translationNotes.note: Elihu is arguing a point about transactions, which is how the friends have framed the whole case: righteousness earns payment, sin incurs debt. His answer in verses 6 to 8 is that God is not a party to that ledger, and that a man's conduct lands on other men. Paul makes the same move with the same logic at Romans 11:35, quoting Job 41:11.

The night was divided into watches kept by real people: shepherds with flocks, city sentries on the wall, travellers waiting for light. Singing through a watch was how the hours were passed and how the watch stayed awake, and Psalm 42:8 and Psalm 77:6 both use it. Elihu's complaint is that men cry out under oppression without ever asking after the One who supplies the song for the long hours.

Shav means emptiness or falsehood and it is the word in the commandment against taking God's name in vain, that is, lifting it onto nothing. Elihu is not saying God ignores suffering; he is saying a cry that is only noise, with no turning behind it, is a cry addressed to nobody. Isaiah 1:15 makes the same charge against raised hands.

translationNotes.term: Wiser than the birds of the air
translationNotes.note: Elihu answers Job's own line at 12:7, where Job sent the friends to learn from the animals. Elihu turns it around: God teaches man more than the beasts and makes him wiser than the birds, so the appeal to animal knowledge cuts the other way. The two verses should be read together, because Elihu is quoting to rebut.

stories.keyTakeaway: Elihu argues that Job's righteousness or sin affects only other people, not God, and contends that God does not answer the arrogant and wicked; he accuses Job of speaking without knowledge.

stories.title: 🗯️ Job 36
summaryBullets: And Elihu continued: (36:1).
“Bear with me a little longer, and I will show you that there is more to be said on God’s behalf. (36:2).
I get my knowledge from afar, and I will ascribe justice to my Maker. (36:3).
For truly my words are free of falsehood; one perfect in knowledge is with you. (36:4).
Indeed, God is mighty, but He despises no one; He is mighty in strength of understanding. (36:5).
He does not keep the wicked alive, but He grants justice to the afflicted. (36:6).
He does not take His eyes off the righteous, but He enthrones them with kings and exalts them forever. (36:7).
And if men are bound with chains, caught in cords of affliction, (36:8).
then He tells them their deeds and how arrogantly they have transgressed. (36:9).
He opens their ears to correction and commands that they turn from iniquity. (36:10).
If they obey and serve Him, then they end their days in prosperity and their years in happiness. (36:11).
But if they do not obey, then they perish by the sword and die without knowledge. (36:12).
The godless in heart harbor resentment; even when He binds them, they do not cry for help. (36:13).
They die in their youth, among the male shrine prostitutes. (36:14).
God rescues the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression. (36:15).
Indeed, He drew you from the jaws of distress to a spacious and broad place, to a table full of richness. (36:16).
But now you are laden with the judgment due the wicked; judgment and justice have seized you. (36:17).
Be careful that no one lures you with riches; do not let a large bribe lead you astray. (36:18).
Can your wealth or all your mighty effort keep you from distress? (36:19).
Do not long for the night, when people vanish from their homes. (36:20).
Be careful not to turn to iniquity, for this you have preferred to affliction. (36:21).
Behold, God is exalted in His power. Who is a teacher like Him? (36:22).
Who has appointed His way for Him, or told Him, ‘You have done wrong’? (36:23).
Remember to magnify His work, which men have praised in song. (36:24).
All mankind has seen it; men behold it from afar. (36:25).
Indeed, God is great — beyond our knowledge; the number of His years is unsearchable. (36:26).
For He draws up drops of water which distill the rain from the mist, (36:27).
which the clouds pour out and shower abundantly on mankind. (36:28).
Furthermore, who can understand how the clouds spread out, how the thunder roars from His pavilion? (36:29).
See how He scatters His lightning around Him and covers the depths of the sea. (36:30).
For by these He judges the nations and provides food in abundance. (36:31).
He fills His hands with lightning and commands it to strike its mark. (36:32).
The thunder declares His presence; even the cattle regard the rising storm. (36:33).
crossRefs: Psalm 25:8-9: He instructs sinners in the way and guides the humble in what is right.
Deuteronomy 8:2-3: He humbled you and let you hunger in the wilderness in order to teach you.
Deuteronomy 23:17-18: No cult prostitute among the sons of Israel, and no such wages brought into the house of the LORD.
Psalm 135:7: He makes clouds rise from the ends of the earth and sends lightning with the rain.
Jeremiah 10:13: When He thunders the waters roar; He brings the wind out of His storehouses.

translationNotes.note: The word means the consecrated ones, and it names men and women attached to a sanctuary whose service to the fertility gods included sexual acts on the premises. The law bans it flatly and forbids bringing the earnings into God's house (Deuteronomy 23:17-18). Kings of Judah kept having to clear them out: Asa, Jehoshaphat and finally Josiah, who tore down their quarters in the temple itself (1 Kings 15:12; 22:46; 2 Kings 23:7). Elihu names the shortest lives he knows of and this is the group he picks.

translationNotes.term: He draws up drops of water
translationNotes.note: Verses 27 and 28 describe evaporation, condensation and rainfall in order: water drawn up, distilled through the mist, poured back out by the clouds. Ecclesiastes 1:7 traces the same circuit through the rivers and back. In a country with no river worth irrigating from except the Jordan, where crops depended on the early and latter rains, this cycle was watched with attention that was not academic.

translationNotes.term: By these He judges the nations and provides food
translationNotes.note: The same storm does both jobs, and Elihu says so in one line. Rain in that climate arrives in two seasons, the early rain of October and November that lets the ground be ploughed and the latter rain of March and April that fills the grain. Miss either and there is famine. Hail and flood in the same clouds destroy the crop. The weather was the economy.

Deshen is fatness, the rich part, and it is used both of the fat of an offering and of a well-fed man's prosperity. Elihu is describing being brought out of a narrow place into a broad one with a laden table, which is the standard Hebrew picture of relief: distress is narrowness and rescue is room (Psalm 18:19; 118:5).

stories.keyTakeaway: Elihu argues that God is mighty and just, using affliction to correct the arrogant and stubborn while delivering those who suffer; he then describes God's power over weather and nations as evidence of his greatness beyond human understanding.

stories.title: 🗯️ Job 37
summaryBullets: “At this my heart also pounds and leaps from its place. (37:1).
Listen closely to the thunder of His voice and the rumbling that comes from His mouth. (37:2).
He unleashes His lightning beneath the whole sky and sends it to the ends of the earth. (37:3).
Then there comes a roaring sound; He thunders with His majestic voice. He does not restrain the lightning when His voice resounds. (37:4).
God thunders wondrously with His voice; He does great things we cannot comprehend. (37:5).
For He says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ and to the gentle rain, ‘Pour out a mighty downpour.’ (37:6).
He seals up the hand of every man, so that all men may know His work. (37:7).
The wild animals enter their lairs; they settle down in their dens. (37:8).
The tempest comes from its chamber, and the cold from the driving north winds. (37:9).
By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen. (37:10).
He loads the clouds with moisture; He scatters His lightning through them. (37:11).
They swirl about, whirling at His direction, accomplishing all that He commands over the face of all the earth. (37:12).
Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His loving devotion. (37:13).
Listen to this, O Job; stand still and consider the wonders of God. (37:14).
Do you know how God dispatches the clouds or makes the lightning flash? (37:15).
Do you understand how the clouds float, those wonders of Him who is perfect in knowledge? (37:16).
You whose clothes get hot when the land lies hushed under the south wind, (37:17).
can you, like Him, spread out the skies, as strong as a mirror of bronze? (37:18).
Teach us what we should say to Him; we cannot draw up our case because of our darkness. (37:19).
Should He be told that I want to speak? Would a man ask to be swallowed up? (37:20).
Now no one can gaze at the sun when it is bright in the skies after the wind has swept them clean. (37:21).
Out of the north He comes in golden splendor; awesome majesty surrounds Him. (37:22).
The Almighty is beyond our reach; He is exalted in power! In His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress. (37:23).
Therefore, men fear Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart.” (37:24).
crossRefs: Psalm 29:3-9: The voice of the LORD over the waters, breaking cedars and shaking the wilderness of Kadesh.
Psalm 147:16-18: He spreads the snow like wool and scatters the frost like ashes, then sends His word and melts them.
Exodus 38:8: The bronze basin and its stand made from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance.
1 Kings 19:11-12: A great wind, an earthquake and a fire pass by, and after them a low whisper.
Job 38:22-23: The LORD asks Job whether he has entered the storehouses of the snow and the hail.

translationNotes.note: Snow was not exotic. It falls most winters on the high ground of Lebanon and Hermon and reaches Jerusalem, 750 metres up, every few years. Hermon holds snow into summer, which is why Jeremiah 18:14 uses it as the byword for something that never fails. Elihu's list of winter weather in verses 6 to 10 is ordinary observation for anyone living above the coastal plain.

translationNotes.term: He seals up the hand of every man
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּיַד-כָּל-אָדָם יַחְתּוֹם (be-yad kol adam yachtom)
translationNotes.note: Winter storms stopped outdoor work. Ploughing, harvest, building and travel all halted while the rain ran, and everyone sat indoors, which is what the line means: God puts a seal on the working hand. Verse 8 pairs it with the animals going into their dens. It is a description of the season shutting down, not of paralysis.

translationNotes.term: Strong as a mirror of bronze
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְאִי מוּצָק (re'i mutsaq), a cast mirror
translationNotes.note: There was no glass mirror. A mirror was a disc of bronze, cast and then polished to a hard bright surface, and Israelite women donated theirs to make the tabernacle basin (Exodus 38:8). Egyptian and Levantine examples survive in museums. The comparison is not about reflection but about the sky being hammered metal: thin, hard and beaten out, which is what the verb spread out means.

translationNotes.term: Out of the north He comes in golden splendour
translationNotes.note: The north is where the winter storm fronts came from, off the Lebanon range, and Elihu has just spent ten verses on that weather. The word tsafon also names the mountain the Canaanites held to be the seat of their storm god Baal, which is why Isaiah 14:13 has a king boasting he will sit on the heights of tsafon. Elihu names the direction the storm comes from and attributes the glory in it to God.

stories.keyTakeaway: Elihu describes God's power over weather and creation - lightning, snow, rain, wind, and ice - all commanded by his voice and beyond human understanding or control. He challenges Job to consider God's wonders and declares that the Almighty is exalted, just, and beyond human reach.

stories.title: 🌪️ Job 38
summaryBullets: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: (38:1).
“Who is this who obscures My counsel by words without knowledge? (38:2).
Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me. (38:3).
Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding. (38:4).
Who fixed its measurements? Surely you know! Or who stretched a measuring line across it? (38:5).
On what were its foundations set, or who laid its cornerstone, (38:6).
while the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy? (38:7).
Who enclosed the sea behind doors when it burst forth from the womb, (38:8).
when I made the clouds its garment and thick darkness its blanket, (38:9).
when I fixed its boundaries and set in place its bars and doors, (38:10).
and I declared: ‘You may come this far, but no farther; here your proud waves must stop’? (38:11).
In your days, have you commanded the morning or assigned the dawn its place, (38:12).
that it might spread to the ends of the earth and shake the wicked out of it? (38:13).
The earth takes shape like clay under a seal; its hills stand out like the folds of a garment. (38:14).
Light is withheld from the wicked, and their upraised arm is broken. (38:15).
Have you journeyed to the vents of the sea or walked in the trenches of the deep? (38:16).
Have the gates of death been revealed to you? Have you seen the gates of the shadow of death? (38:17).
Have you surveyed the extent of the earth? Tell Me, if you know all this. (38:18).
Where is the way to the home of light? Do you know where darkness resides, (38:19).
so you can lead it back to its border? Do you know the paths to its home? (38:20).
Surely you know, for you were already born! And the number of your days is great! (38:21).
Have you entered the storehouses of snow or observed the storehouses of hail, (38:22).
which I hold in reserve for times of trouble, for the day of war and battle? (38:23).
In which direction is the lightning dispersed, or the east wind scattered over the earth? (38:24).
Who cuts a channel for the flood or clears a path for the thunderbolt, (38:25).
to bring rain on a barren land, on a desert where no man lives, (38:26).
to satisfy the parched wasteland and make it sprout with tender grass? (38:27).
Does the rain have a father? Who has begotten the drops of dew? (38:28).
From whose womb does the ice emerge? Who gives birth to the frost from heaven, (38:29).
when the waters become hard as stone and the surface of the deep is frozen? (38:30).
Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loosen the belt of Orion? (38:31).
Can you bring forth the constellations in their seasons or lead out the Bear and her cubs? (38:32).
Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you set their dominion over the earth? (38:33).
Can you command the clouds so that a flood of water covers you? (38:34).
Can you send the lightning bolts on their way? Do they report to you, ‘Here we are’? (38:35).
Who has put wisdom in the heart or given understanding to the mind? (38:36).
Who has the wisdom to count the clouds? Or who can tilt the water jars of the heavens (38:37).
when the dust hardens into a mass and the clods of earth stick together? (38:38).
Can you hunt the prey for a lioness or satisfy the hunger of young lions (38:39).
when they crouch in their dens and lie in wait in the thicket? (38:40).
Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food? (38:41).
crossRefs: Genesis 1:1-10: God makes the heavens and the earth, separates the waters, and gathers the sea into its place.
Proverbs 8:27-29: When He set the heavens in place, marked the horizon on the deep and set the sea its limit.
Amos 5:8: He who made the Pleiades and Orion, and turns midnight into dawn and day into night.
Psalm 147:9: He gives the animals their food and feeds the young ravens when they cry.
Jeremiah 5:22: I made the sand a boundary for the sea, an everlasting barrier it cannot cross.

translationNotes.note: A violent storm wind, not a tornado in the modern sense. It is the wind that takes Elijah up (2 Kings 2:1,11), the wind of the LORD going out in fury (Jeremiah 23:19), and the wind Jonah's sailors are caught in (Jonah 1:4). Elihu has just spent two chapters describing an approaching storm; the answer arrives out of the weather he was pointing at.

Verses 4 to 6 are a building site: measurements taken, a line stretched, footings sunk, a cornerstone set. A cornerstone was the first dressed block laid at a corner, and every other course was aligned from it, so getting it wrong meant the whole wall ran out of true. Foundation deposits were laid with ceremony in the ancient Near East, which is why verse 7 has singing at the moment it goes down.

The Pleiades is a tight open cluster in Taurus, about 440 light-years away, of which six or seven stars are visible without a telescope, and the chains binding them are that clustering. Orion is a spread of bright stars with three in a row at its belt, and loosening his belt is undoing that line. Their risings and settings fixed the farming year all round the Mediterranean; the Greek poet Hesiod, writing about 700 BC, tells farmers to harvest when the Pleiades rise and plough when they set.

This word occurs once in the Bible and its exact reference is not established; it is rendered constellations here and left untranslated as Mazzaroth in older versions. A related form, mazzalot, appears at 2 Kings 23:5 among the things Josiah's reform removed, where it clearly means star groups worshipped alongside the sun and moon. The Bear and her cubs in the same verse is the group English calls the Plough or the Big Dipper.

An otsar is a storehouse or treasury, the walled room where a king kept grain, silver and weapons under seal. The picture is of weather held in a locked armoury and issued when needed, and verse 23 says what it is reserved for: the day of battle and war. Joshua 10:11 records exactly that use, hailstones killing more of the enemy than the sword did.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD speaks to Job from a storm, challenging him with a series of rhetorical questions about creation - where Job was when the earth's foundation was laid, whether he controls weather and celestial bodies, and whether he provides for wild animals - implying Job lacks the knowledge and power to question God's plans.

stories.title: 🌪️ Job 39
summaryBullets: “Do you know when mountain goats give birth? Have you watched the doe bear her fawn? (39:1).
Can you count the months they are pregnant? Do you know the time they give birth? (39:2).
They crouch down and bring forth their young; they deliver their newborn. (39:3).
Their young ones thrive and grow up in the open field; they leave and do not return. (39:4).
Who set the wild donkey free? Who released the swift donkey from the harness? (39:5).
I made the wilderness his home and the salt flats his dwelling. (39:6).
He scorns the tumult of the city and never hears the shouts of a driver. (39:7).
He roams the mountains for pasture, searching for any green thing. (39:8).
Will the wild ox consent to serve you? Will he stay by your manger at night? (39:9).
Can you hold him to the furrow with a harness? Will he plow the valleys behind you? (39:10).
Can you rely on his great strength? Will you leave your hard work to him? (39:11).
Can you trust him to bring in your grain and gather it to your threshing floor? (39:12).
The wings of the ostrich flap joyfully, but cannot match the pinions and feathers of the stork. (39:13).
For she leaves her eggs on the ground and lets them warm in the sand. (39:14).
She forgets that a foot may crush them, or a wild animal may trample them. (39:15).
She treats her young harshly, as if not her own, with no concern that her labor was in vain. (39:16).
For God has deprived her of wisdom; He has not endowed her with understanding. (39:17).
Yet when she proudly spreads her wings, she laughs at the horse and its rider. (39:18).
Do you give strength to the horse or adorn his neck with a mane? (39:19).
Do you make him leap like a locust, striking terror with his proud snorting? (39:20).
He paws in the valley and rejoices in his strength; he charges into battle. (39:21).
He laughs at fear, frightened of nothing; he does not turn back from the sword. (39:22).
A quiver rattles at his side, along with a flashing spear and lance. (39:23).
Trembling with excitement, he devours the distance; he cannot stand still when the ram’s horn sounds. (39:24).
At the blast of the horn, he snorts with fervor. He catches the scent of battle from afar, the shouts of captains and the cry of war. (39:25).
Does the hawk take flight by your understanding and spread his wings toward the south? (39:26).
Does the eagle soar at your command and make his nest on high? (39:27).
He dwells on a cliff and lodges there; his stronghold is on a rocky crag. (39:28).
From there he spies out food; his eyes see it from afar. (39:29).
His young ones feast on blood; and where the slain are, there he is.” (39:30).
crossRefs: Psalm 104:16-22: The high mountains belong to the wild goats, and the young lions seek their food from God.
Numbers 23:22: God brought them out of Egypt with strength like that of a wild ox.
Lamentations 4:3: Even jackals nurse their young, but my people have become cruel, like ostriches in the wilderness.
Jeremiah 8:7: Even the stork in the sky knows her appointed seasons, and the dove keeps the time of her coming.
Proverbs 21:31: The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the LORD.

translationNotes.note: The aurochs, Bos primigenius, the wild ancestor of domestic cattle, standing about 1.8 metres at the shoulder with forward-curving horns. Assyrian kings recorded hunting it and it survived in Europe until the last recorded animal died in a Polish forest in 1627. The Greek Old Testament rendered re'em as monokeros, one-horn, and that is how unicorn entered the King James Version at Numbers 23:22 and Job 39:9. The point of verses 9 to 12 is that this is a bull nobody could put in a yoke.

The Arabian ostrich lived across the Syrian and Arabian deserts until hunting wiped it out in the middle of the twentieth century. The behaviour described in verses 14 to 16 is accurate: the eggs go into a shallow scrape in open ground, several hens lay in the same nest, and eggs outside the main clutch are left to the sun and are trampled or lost. Verse 18 is also accurate: an ostrich runs at about 70 kilometres an hour, which no horse can hold.

translationNotes.term: Adorn his neck with a mane
translationNotes.note: The noun comes from the root for thunder, so the word for the horse's neck covering is built on the sound of a storm. English has to pick one word and loses the other. Horses in this period were driven in chariots and used by couriers rather than ridden in massed cavalry, which came later; the animal in verses 19 to 25 is a chariot horse, harnessed beside another, with a driver and a fighting man aboard.

A shofar is a horn, not a manufactured trumpet: a ram's or wild goat's horn softened, straightened at the mouth and blown. It has no fingerholes and gives two or three notes, so it signals rather than plays. It was the battlefield instrument that started a charge and sounded a retreat (Judges 7:16-22; 2 Samuel 2:28). Verses 24 and 25 describe a trained warhorse reacting to that signal before the rider does.

translationNotes.term: Where the slain are, there he is
translationNotes.note: The word means those run through, that is, battlefield dead. Eagles and vultures following an army were an ordinary sight and a fixed image for the aftermath of a defeat (Deuteronomy 28:26; Ezekiel 39:17-20). Jesus quotes the proverb in the same shape: where the corpse is, there the vultures gather (Matthew 24:28).

stories.keyTakeaway: God describes wild animals and birds that exist beyond human control: mountain goats, wild donkeys, wild oxen, ostriches, horses, hawks, and eagles, each with their own instincts and habitats. The point is that Job does not govern these creatures; they live according to their nature, not human design.

headings.text: The Lord Speaks of His Creation

stories.title: 🌪️ Job 40
summaryBullets: And the LORD said to Job: (40:1).
“Will the faultfinder contend with the Almighty? Let him who argues with God give an answer.” (40:2).
Then Job answered the LORD: (40:3).
“Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth. (40:4).
I have spoken once, but I have no answer — twice, but I have nothing to add.” (40:5).
Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: (40:6).
“Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me. (40:7).
Would you really annul My justice? Would you condemn Me to justify yourself? (40:8).
Do you have an arm like God’s? Can you thunder with a voice like His? (40:9).
Then adorn yourself with majesty and splendor, and clothe yourself with honor and glory. (40:10).
Unleash the fury of your wrath; look on every proud man and bring him low. (40:11).
Look on every proud man and humble him; trample the wicked where they stand. (40:12).
Bury them together in the dust; imprison them in the grave. (40:13).
Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you. (40:14).
Look at Behemoth, which I made along with you. He feeds on grass like an ox. (40:15).
See the strength of his loins and the power in the muscles of his belly. (40:16).
His tail sways like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are tightly knit. (40:17).
His bones are tubes of bronze; his limbs are rods of iron. (40:18).
He is the foremost of God’s works; only his Maker can draw the sword against him. (40:19).
The hills yield him their produce, while all the beasts of the field play nearby. (40:20).
He lies under the lotus plants, hidden among the reeds of the marsh. (40:21).
The lotus plants conceal him in their shade; the willows of the brook surround him. (40:22).
Though the river rages, Behemoth is unafraid; he remains secure, though the Jordan surges to his mouth. (40:23).
Can anyone capture him as he looks on, or pierce his nose with a snare? (40:24).
crossRefs: Job 42:1-6: Job's final answer, where he takes back what he said and repents in dust and ashes.
Psalm 39:9: I was silent; I did not open my mouth, because it was You who did it.
Psalm 50:10-11: Every animal of the forest is Mine, and the cattle on a thousand hills.
Genesis 1:24-25: God makes the livestock and the wild animals of the earth, each according to its kind.
Isaiah 45:9: Woe to the one who quarrels with his Maker, a potsherd among the potsherds of the earth.

translationNotes.term: I place my hand over my mouth
translationNotes.note: The formal gesture of yielding the floor, used when a man has nothing further he is entitled to say. Job demanded it of his friends at 21:5, princes did it in his presence in his prime (29:9), and here he performs it himself. It is the physical counterpart of verse 5: I have spoken once, and twice, and I will not add.

The word is the plural of behemah, an animal or beast, used here of a single creature; Hebrew does that to mean the beast of all beasts, the supreme example. What the text says about it is specific: it eats grass like an ox, its strength is in its loins and belly, its tail moves like a cedar, its bones are like tubes of bronze, it lies in the marsh under the lotus among the reeds, and it is unmoved when the river runs hard at it (40:15-24). Readers have identified it with the hippopotamus, which lived in the lower Nile until it was hunted out in the nineteenth century, and others with an animal now known only from bones. The text names no species.

Reshit means the first or chief of a series, the same word that opens Genesis 1:1 and that names the firstfruits of a harvest. The line places this animal at the head of the created works being paraded, and the second half of the verse says only its Maker can bring a sword against it. It is the setup for chapter 41, where the creature cannot be taken at all.

translationNotes.term: Pierce his nose with a snare
translationNotes.note: Large animals were controlled by a ring or hook through the nose or lip, the way cattle still are, and Assyrian reliefs show prisoners of war led by exactly that. 2 Kings 19:28 has God saying He will put a hook in Sennacherib's nose. The challenge in verse 24 is whether Job can do to Behemoth what a herdsman does to an ox, and chapter 41 asks the same question of Leviathan five different ways.

stories.keyTakeaway: God challenges Job to answer whether he can do what God does - rule with justice and power; then God describes Behemoth, a massive creature he made, to illustrate his mastery over creation.

headings.text: Job Humbles Himself before the Lord

stories.title: 🌪️ Job 41
summaryBullets: “Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook or tie down his tongue with a rope? (41:1).
Can you put a cord through his nose or pierce his jaw with a hook? (41:2).
Will he beg you for mercy or speak to you softly? (41:3).
Will he make a covenant with you to take him as a slave for life? (41:4).
Can you pet him like a bird or put him on a leash for your maidens? (41:5).
Will traders barter for him or divide him among the merchants? (41:6).
Can you fill his hide with harpoons or his head with fishing spears? (41:7).
If you lay a hand on him, you will remember the battle and never repeat it! (41:8).
Surely hope of overcoming him is false. Is not the sight of him overwhelming? (41:9).
No one is so fierce as to rouse Leviathan. Then who is able to stand against Me? (41:10).
Who has given to Me that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is Mine. (41:11).
I cannot keep silent about his limbs, his power and graceful form. (41:12).
Who can strip off his outer coat? Who can approach him with a bridle? (41:13).
Who can open his jaws, ringed by his fearsome teeth? (41:14).
His rows of scales are his pride, tightly sealed together. (41:15).
One scale is so near to another that no air can pass between them. (41:16).
They are joined to one another; they clasp and cannot be separated. (41:17).
His snorting flashes with light, and his eyes are like the rays of dawn. (41:18).
Firebrands stream from his mouth; fiery sparks shoot forth! (41:19).
Smoke billows from his nostrils as from a boiling pot over burning reeds. (41:20).
His breath sets coals ablaze, and flames pour from his mouth. (41:21).
Strength resides in his neck, and dismay leaps before him. (41:22).
The folds of his flesh are tightly joined; they are firm and immovable. (41:23).
His chest is as hard as a rock, as hard as a lower millstone! (41:24).
When Leviathan rises up, the mighty are terrified; they withdraw before his thrashing. (41:25).
The sword that reaches him has no effect, nor does the spear or dart or arrow. (41:26).
He regards iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood. (41:27).
No arrow can make him flee; slingstones become like chaff to him. (41:28).
A club is regarded as straw, and he laughs at the sound of the lance. (41:29).
His undersides are jagged potsherds, spreading out the mud like a threshing sledge. (41:30).
He makes the depths seethe like a cauldron; he makes the sea like a jar of ointment. (41:31).
He leaves a glistening wake behind him; one would think the deep had white hair! (41:32).
Nothing on earth is his equal— a creature devoid of fear! (41:33).
He looks down on all the haughty; he is king over all the proud.” (41:34).
crossRefs: Psalm 104:25-26: The sea teems with creatures beyond number, and Leviathan frolics in it.
Psalm 74:13-14: You broke the heads of the sea monsters and crushed the heads of Leviathan.
Isaiah 27:1: The LORD will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the coiling serpent.
Job 3:8: Job called on those who curse days and who are ready to rouse Leviathan.
Romans 11:35: Paul quotes Job 41:11, who has ever given to God, that God should repay him?

translationNotes.note: The chapter describes a water creature with rows of scales sealed so tightly that no air passes between them, a chest as hard as a lower millstone, an underside like broken pottery that scores the mud like a threshing sledge, and a hide no sword, spear, arrow, club or slingstone will get through (41:15-30). Readers have identified it with the Nile crocodile, which grows to about five metres and drags exactly that ridged track; crocodiles survived on the coast of the land itself, in the stream still called Nahal Taninim north of Caesarea, until they were shot out in the early twentieth century. The text names no species and adds detail no crocodile answers to.

Verses 1 to 8 run through every method used to take a large water animal: hook and line, a cord through the nose, a rope on the tongue, a leash, a barbed harpoon, a fish spear. Egyptian tomb paintings show hippopotamus hunting with harpoons and float lines exactly as described. The whole passage is a list of professional techniques and a verdict that all of them fail.

A hand mill had two stones. The upper one turned and the lower one sat still and took every stroke, so it was cut from the hardest, densest rock available, usually basalt, and it outlasted the mill. That is the comparison for the creature's chest. The law forbids taking either millstone in pledge, because a family without a mill cannot eat (Deuteronomy 24:6).

A heavy wooden sledge with sharp flints or iron teeth set into its underside, weighted with the driver standing on it and dragged by oxen round and round the threshing floor to cut the straw and free the grain. Examples with the flints still in place survive. Isaiah 41:15 uses one as an image of a new sharp threshing sledge with many teeth. Verse 30 says the animal's belly plates leave the mud looking as if one had been dragged over it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּנֵי-שָׁחַץ (benei-shachats), the sons of pride
translationNotes.note: The phrase appears twice, at 28:8 where it means the proud beasts that have never walked the miner's path, and here at the very end. So the creature's title is king over the strongest wild animals there are. It is the last line of God's speech, and the argument closes on a creature Job cannot even approach, let alone summon to court.

stories.keyTakeaway: God describes Leviathan in exhaustive detail - its impenetrable armor, fiery breath, and invulnerability to human weapons - and concludes that nothing on earth equals this creature and it reigns over all the proud.

headings.text: The Lord’s Power Shown in Leviathan

stories.title: 🌿 Job 42
summaryBullets: Then Job replied to the LORD: (42:1).
“I know that You can do all things and that no plan of Yours can be thwarted. (42:2).
You asked, ‘Who is this who conceals My counsel without knowledge?’ Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know. (42:3).
You said, ‘Listen now, and I will speak. I will question you, and you shall inform Me.’ (42:4).
My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You. (42:5).
Therefore I despise myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.” (42:6).

After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has. (42:7).

So now, take seven bulls and seven rams, go to My servant Job, and sacrifice a burnt offering for yourselves. Then My servant Job will pray for you, for I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken accurately about Me, as My servant Job has.” (42:8).
So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the LORD had told them; and the LORD accepted Job’s prayer. (42:9).
After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his prosperity and doubled his former possessions. (42:10).

All his brothers and sisters and prior acquaintances came and dined with him in his house. They consoled him and comforted him over all the adversity that the LORD had brought upon him. And each one gave him a piece of silver and a gold ring. (42:11).
So the LORD blessed Job’s latter days more than his first. He owned 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys. (42:12).
And he also had seven sons and three daughters. (42:13).
He named his first daughter Jemimah, his second Keziah, and his third Keren-happuch. (42:14).
No women as beautiful as Job’s daughters could be found in all the land, and their father granted them an inheritance among their brothers. (42:15).
After this, Job lived 140 years and saw his children and their children to the fourth generation. (42:16).
And so Job died, old and full of years. (42:17).
crossRefs: Genesis 33:19: Jacob buys the plot of ground at Shechem from the sons of Hamor for a hundred kesitah.
Joshua 24:32: Joseph's bones are buried in that same plot, bought for a hundred kesitah.
Numbers 27:1-11: The daughters of Zelophehad ask for a share of the inheritance and are granted one.
Exodus 22:4: A thief caught with the animal alive must repay double what he took.
James 5:11: You have heard of Job's perseverance and have seen what the Lord finally brought about.

translationNotes.note: An archaic unit of money that appears three times in the whole Bible, and only here and in two verses about one transaction: Jacob buys ground at Shechem for a hundred kesitah (Genesis 33:19), and Joseph is buried in it (Joshua 24:32). Its weight is not known. The Greek translators of the third and second centuries BC rendered it lamb, which points to a weight of silver reckoned against the price of a sheep. Its use here is one more mark that this book's world is the patriarchs' world, not Israel's.

A nezem is a ring worn in the nose or the ear. Abraham's servant gives Rebekah one weighing a beka, about 5.7 grams (Genesis 24:22), and Gideon collects 1,700 shekels of gold in captured earrings, about 19 kilograms (Judges 8:26). Before coinage, jewellery was money you could wear: valued by weight, and cut or melted when it had to be spent. Each visitor gives Job a coin-weight and a wearable ingot.

The arithmetic is exact. Chapter 1 lists 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen and 500 female donkeys; verse 12 lists 14,000, 6,000, 1,000 yoke and 1,000, each precisely twice. Double restitution is the law's penalty for theft (Exodus 22:4,7,9). The children are the one item not doubled: seven sons and three daughters again, the same count as 1:2.

Daughters normally received a dowry, not a share of the estate; property passed through sons to keep land in the clan. Israel's law later allowed daughters to inherit only where there was no son at all, and even then required them to marry within their own tribe (Numbers 27:1-11; 36:6-9). Job has seven sons and still gives his three daughters a share alongside them, which is not the ordinary practice in any period of the Old Testament.

translationNotes.note: These are the only children named in the book. Keziah means cassia, an aromatic bark related to cinnamon and one of the ingredients of the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:24). Keren-happuch means horn of eye paint: puk is the black cosmetic, ground galena, that women applied around the eyes with a stick from a small horn or jar. Jezebel paints her eyes with it (2 Kings 9:30). The names are perfume and cosmetics, the goods of a restored house.

stories.keyTakeaway: God rebukes the friends and accepts Job’s intercession for them. Job is restored with double livestock, honored by family, and given long life. The story does not record that Job is told the heavenly reason for his suffering.

headings.text: Job Submits Himself to the Lord

intro:
Job does not name its author. Jewish tradition (preserved in the Talmud, Baba Bathra 15a-b) attributes the book to Moses, who may have composed it during his forty years in Midian shepherding for Jethro before God called him at the burning bush. The traditional date of composition places Job among the oldest books of the Bible, written in the 15th century BC. The events recorded are even older, set in the patriarchal era (roughly 2000-1800 BC, the time of Abraham), evidenced by the archaic Hebrew of the text, wealth measured in livestock rather than coin (a patriarchal-era marker), the practice of the head of the family offering sacrifices without any reference to the Levitical priesthood (which did not yet exist), no mention of the Law of Moses or the Exodus, and patriarchal-era longevity. Job lived in the land of Uz, traditionally identified with northern Arabia or the region of Edom, east and southeast of the future land of Israel. The historical setting of the events is the Bronze Age, before the Israelite nation existed; Egypt was in the Middle Kingdom or early New Kingdom era, the Hittite Empire was emerging in Anatolia, and the patriarchal tribes of the Semitic peoples lived as nomadic pastoralists across the Levant, Arabia, and Mesopotamia. Moses, who according to tradition compiled the book, was born in Egypt to Hebrew slaves of the tribe of Levi, raised in Pharaoh's household with a full Egyptian education, fled to Midian after killing an Egyptian taskmaster, and lived as a shepherd for forty years among the Midianites in northwestern Arabia, a region adjacent to the land of Uz where Job's story is set.

Job is the eighteenth book of the Christian Old Testament. In the Hebrew Bible it is part of the Ketuvim (Writings). The Hebrew name Iyyov (אִיּוֹב) may derive from a root meaning "one persecuted" or "the hated one," though the etymology is uncertain and may reflect a non-Hebrew origin from the land of Uz. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Job were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 2nd and 1st centuries BC; the Qumran community also produced a Targum (Aramaic translation) of Job, indicating early interest in this ancient text.
